articles.title: The end of Maga as we know it
articles.summary:
The Republican party will regroup after their shellacking in the US midterm elections, but it won’t look the same

Walking by a tattoo studio and medical spa on the pretty main street of
articles.byline: David Smith in Round Rock, Texas

blocks.text: Walking by a tattoo studio and medical spa on the pretty main street of Round Rock, in Texas Hill Country, Tarik Bakir recalled voting for Barack Obama in 2008 and Donald Trump in 2024. But when it came to the 2026 midterm elections, he was firmly back in the Democrats’ column.

“I’m not happy with the Iran war,” said Bakir, 41, a financial adviser who served with the US military in Afghanistan. “The economy’s OK, but not great. This election was a rebuttal to Trump. This time people said they didn’t like him, or his policies.”

Once a reliably Republican suburb north of Austin, Round Rock is the birthplace of James Talarico, whose victory this week in a US Senate election – Democrats’ first in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born – symbolised a nationwide “blue-nami” that swept away Trump’s Maga (Make America Great Again) coalition.

It was the most sweeping midterm repudiation of a sitting president since the Watergate election of 1974. Unlike typical midterms, where losses are concentrated in swing districts or isolated suburban pockets, the 2026 midterms saw the Republican floor drop out across deep-red strongholds, suburban corridors and rural heartlands alike.

blocks.caption: An election night event for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, in Austin, Texas, on 3 November. Photograph: Ashley Landis/AP

blocks.text: Democrats stormed once impregnable fortresses such as Kansas and South Carolina, taking control of both chambers of Congress and redrawing the political map. In Texas, for decades a bedrock of conservatism, the senator Ted Cruz is now the last statewide Republican still standing.

For Trump, it was a scathing rebuke after a madcap campaign that left some wondering: if the president had deliberately tried to sabotage his own party’s chances, what, precisely, would he have done any differently?

The president heaped praise on Ohio senator Jon Husted’s “ass” but, in the words of Cruz, his party got an “ass-kicking”. Florida governor Ron DeSantis called it “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country”.

Patrick Gaspard, a former official in Barack Obama’s White House, said: “Anyone who says that they were not surprised is lying. This busted all of the models across all demographics and geography. You would think that 2024 was the last century, not just two years ago.”
Why did Maga fall apart so fast, and in such colossal fashion? The short answer is that costs, corruption and conflict with Iran left Trump supporters feeling betrayed.
Frank Luntz, a veteran pollster and strategist, hosted a focus group on the eve of the election with people who voted for Trump in 2024, but would be voting for Democrats in 2026.

Affordability issues were “hurting Trump voters more than others because they are more likely to be paycheck-to-paycheck voters”, said Luntz. “They are more likely to have no money at the end of the week, and very little money at the end of the month, and so they were susceptible to food and fuel prices more than the average voter.”

“They were promised in 2024 that prices would come down, and we wouldn’t have forever wars, that we would drain the swamp,” Luntz added. “They looked in 2026 and they felt not nearly enough had been accomplished on this and so they wanted to punish Republicans. This is not about rewarding Democrats. This was about holding Republicans accountable for these voters believing what they were promised.”

blocks.caption: Political signs in Dallas, Texas, on 3 November. Photograph: Adam Gray/Getty Images

blocks.text: ‘His fingerprints are all around’

Instead of focusing on the economic pressures hurting many of his own supporters, like farmers struggling to pay for diesel and fertiliser, Trump diverted his public commentary towards vanity projects, legal grievances and high-profile spats.

“He lost the plot,” according to Luntz. “He was talking about topics that they didn’t fully understand and didn’t care about. He wasn’t talking about the things that mattered most to them and in the end they took it out on the Republican party.”

Gaspard, a distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington, agrees that the Maga coalition fractured because Trump violated every pledge made to working-class voters – from sweeping tariffs on foreign goods and an unpopular military conflict in Iran to cryptocurrency self-enrichment schemes and federal immigration overreach that terrorised local communities.

The result has broken the psychological chokehold Trump exerted over his party, Gaspard believes. “We’re seeing it already. When your approval hits the low 30s, politicians think about survival,” he said. “What happened creates a permission structure finally for Republicans to develop a spine to move away from him on their political choices, their policy choices and how they navigate their cultural choices as well.”

He added: “Donald Trump can’t act as if he wasn’t present at the scene of the crime. He personally picked the candidates in Texas and South Carolina. His fingerprints are all around it, and he can’t proclaim his innocence.”

blocks.caption: Donald Trump during a campaign event in San Antonio, Texas, on 7 October. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Republicans lost most of Trump’s gains with Latino voters in 2024, according to an Associated Press voter poll, while only about one in 10 Black men voted Republican in their local House race, down from roughly one in four who backed Trump in 2024. Voters under 30, who had been roughly evenly divided between Trump and Kamala Harris two years ago, backed Democratic House candidates by about seven-to-three this time.

Gaspard noted that the collapse extended to Trump’s prized demographic strongholds: “When you end up in an election where the Republican party ended up splitting men 50/50 with Democrats, that is a death knell for the manosphere, the bro platforms that they saw as their firewalls.”

Some observers were quick to pronounce the death of Maga and the end of the Trump era. But the past decade of US politics has been characterised by whiplash elections with both parties lurching between triumph and disaster. Trump was written off after his defeat in 2020 only to bounce back four years later. He still has more than 800 days left in office.

Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Is this the end of Maga? No. As long as Donald Trump is in the White House, it’s still a danger. But it’s been badly wounded and, like a cornered ferret, it can still be quite dangerous. But this is a collapse of generational significance across the map and it has to deliver a massive shock to a Republican party that has been enthralled to Donald Trump for 10 years.”

Sykes, author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, added: “It takes a massive defeat like this for a political party to come to its senses. That’s what history tells us. It’s not because of op-ed pieces or commentators, or critical podcasts. It’s losing on this kind of epic level.”

The populist right may have lost some recent battles in Brazil, Serbia and Hungary, where close Maga ally Viktor Orbán was defeated, but it has hardly lost the war. From Argentina to India, its leaders remain in power, while in France, Germany and Britain its movements are challenging the established political order.
‘Like a cornered ferret’

Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, cautioned against assuming that the midterms marked the permanent demise of populist conservatism, comparing its persistence to illiberal movements in Europe.

He said: “I would hesitate to say that it’s the end of Maga, any more than the defeat of Viktor Orbán means the permanent defeat of illiberal democracy, any more than Donald Tusk’s comeback in Poland means that the forces arrayed against him have gone away.

“Maga has deep social roots in the American population. It expresses something that’s real and isn’t going away. But the question is whether it will be as dominant as it has been for more than a decade inside the Republican party in the United States and around the world. I think the answer to that question is no.”

blocks.caption: An election night event for Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, on 3 November. Photograph: Charlie Neibergall/AP

blocks.text: Galston does believe that the midterms have created a vacuum within the Republican party and an opening for a reform candidate to challenge the Maga orthodoxy before 2028.

“These questions are never settled in the abstract,” he continued. “They’re settled when someone steps forward and says: ‘I stand for something different,’ and then convinces enough people that that is the right thing to stand for. That’s the way Donald Trump took the party away from the Reaganites.
“I don’t think we’re going back to the status quo ante, but is somebody going to stand up with a coherent counter-agenda? I don’t know who that would be but there’s a market opportunity.”

Trump responded to his humiliation at the ballot box like a man in denial. The following morning, he retreated to his safe space, the construction site of a new White House ballroom, and concentrated on signing a structural beam rather than addressing the electoral defeat. “Trump is still your president,” read an official White House social media post superimposed over an image of the 80-year-old, glowering into the camera.

But the race to succeed him has been blown wide open by the Republican debacle. Newt Gingrich, a former speaker of the House, wrote on social media: “The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open.”

The biggest loser was the vice-president, JD Vance, who responded by posting an essay-length message on X, publicly identifying Trump’s deeply unpopular war in Iran as the catalyst for the defeat. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in what many saw as a calculated move to align himself with rightwing podcasters – and to put daylight between himself and his boss.

blocks.caption: JD Vance in Hendersonville, North Carolina, on 19 October. Photograph: Kenny Holston/The New York Times/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “It’s going to be very challenging for JD Vance, because he’s hitched his wagon to Donald Trump so closely as his vice-president. But he’s going to try: he’s a professional political chameleon. I don’t think he has the chops to do it. He’s not very good at this.”

Other Republican contenders for 2028 could include DeSantis; Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Nikki Haley, the former US ambassador to the United Nations; Utah governor Spencer Cox; and former Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin. Winning the nomination may depend on harnessing Maga populism while also presenting a new vision.

“Trump is a toxic brand, underwater with every demographic, including his own base,” added Setmayer. “It’s fair to say it’s the end of Maga as we know it under Donald Trump. Be prepared for it to morph into something else with the same basic foundation.”

For Democrats, the challenge meanwhile will be to turn an anti-Trump coalition into a positive political programme. The midterms highlighted a new wave of young, dynamic leaders including Talarico in Texas, Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, a progressive and the first Muslim elected to the Senate. His victory could encourage the representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to throw her hat into the ring in 2028.
‘Our economy’s hurting’
Galston believes that the sweeping wins across deep-red states have effectively rendered traditional debates over candidate “electability” obsolete in the upcoming Democratic primary contest.

“There was something for everyone,” he said. “The arguments over electability have been mooted because it turns out that different kinds of Democrats can win in different kinds of places. That’s good news because, rather than shadow-boxing about electability, Democrats can actually have the discussion that they need substantively.”

blocks.caption: Donald Trump passes out Maga caps during a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on 27 October. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: They will be aware that Trump has an unearthly survival instinct. He has weathered controversies, impeachments, assassination attempts, criminal charges and electoral defeats and is not yet halfway through his second term. But this week’s national reckoning suggests that, after pulling off a comeback for the ages in 2024, he has squandered his last shreds of political capital.
Back in Round Rock in Texas, the epicentre of this week’s electoral tremors, there was little sympathy for the president.

On Main Street, Billy Joe Wilson, 47, who was wearing a long beard, tattooed arms and a bright yellow T-shirt, said: “The guy’s given us six years now of who he is and we keep believing him, and yet everything he says is going the opposite way: gas is up, diesel is up, cost of goods is up. Our economy’s hurting.”

Wilson, who runs bars and restaurants in the area, added: “Texas was a big supporter of the Republican party and Trump. But my generation got tired of realising that we’re getting screwed in the deal. We want to make sure that our kids or grandkids are set up to be successful, not living under a rule where the rich eat the poor.”

articles.title: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
articles.summary: Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump

blocks.text: The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.
But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.
The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”
“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”
Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.
His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.
Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.
“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.
On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”
Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.
After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.
That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.

External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

articles.title: Bigger bank, broader base: TG Limcaoco’s BPI years
articles.summary: From overseeing a bank merger to scrapping transfer fees and bringing banking into neighborhood stores, it's been a busy five years for Limcaoco

blocks.text: LAST DANCE? BPI president and CEO TG Limcaoco speaks at the bank's 175th gala on October 26, 2026.
BPI
From overseeing a bank merger to scrapping transfer fees and bringing banking into neighborhood stores, it's been a busy five years for Limcaoco

items: Jose Teodoro 'TG' Limcaoco will step down as president and CEO of the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) in April 2027, transitioning to a senior role within the Ayala Group.

Under Limcaoco's leadership, BPI's annual net income increased significantly, and the bank expanded its customer base and services, including the introduction of free money transfers and agency banking.

Limcaoco emphasized the importance of financial inclusion and expressed concerns about the limited access to formal financial services for many Filipinos, while also engaging with the community through initiatives like a Disney-themed savings account for children.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
After five years at the helm of the 175-year-old Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco is ready to say goodbye to the country’s oldest bank.

Limcaoco will step down as president and chief executive officer in April 2027, making way for consumer banking chief Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go, BPI’s first female CEO. He will remain on the board and take on other senior roles within the Ayala Group.

Five years is a short chapter for a bank that has survived colonial governments, wars, and economic crises. But Limcaoco was hardly new to BPI or the Ayalas when he took the helm in 2021. He had been president of BPI Capital and BPI Family Savings Bank, then spent six years as Ayala Corporation’s chief financial officer.
The bank he inherited from Cezar “Bong” Consing was already one of the country’s largest. The one he will leave behind is considerably bigger.

BPI’s annual net income rose from P23.88 billion in 2021 to P66.62 billion in 2025, while assets grew from P2.42 trillion at end-2021 to P3.9 trillion by September 2026. Its customer base more than doubled to over 19 million, helped in part by the 2024 merger with Robinsons Bank.

But enough of the numbers, and back to the man of the hour. Limcaoco isn’t your typical banker who shies away from the media. He’s frank, sometimes even blunt, and always ready to break down a tough banking topic with an example or two.

Ask him about bank secrecy, and he’ll point out that few countries have laws as restrictive as the Philippines’. Ask about reserve requirements, and he’ll explain why he prefers interest rates as a monetary policy tool.
When Rappler asked last July why BPI made transfers free, he explained that under new central bank rules, it could charge only around P1.50. Why bother customers over that amount?
“You’re just needling the customer,” he said.

BPI became one of the first major commercial banks to permanently waive InstaPay and PESONet fees, with others following with cuts of their own. There was a business case, too. Free transfers could keep customers using BPI and perhaps bring in more business.

Much the same thinking has gone into the bank’s expansion into agency banking under Limcaoco. Customers can now open accounts, deposit, and withdraw money at participating supermarkets and convenience stores — often for free — while BPI avoids some of the costs of branches and ATMs.
In a March interview with McKinsey, Limcaoco summed it up: “Our philosophy is, if you cannot come to the bank, we will bring the bank to you.”
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Deputy Governor Bernadette Romulo-Puyat, who has taken a particular interest in the program, had some rather warm words for Limcaoco.

“Ang galing ni TG (TG’s great),” she told Rappler in a recent chat about financial inclusion. “My experience with him, he was really looking for ways to help give everybody a bank account. He’s made it so simple.”

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] The bank Ginbee Go will inherit

blocks.text: At BPI’s 175th anniversary gala in October, chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala credited Limcaoco with bringing “real dynamism” to the bank, while welcoming to its next chapter under Go.
Limcaoco, meanwhile, spent much of his own speech looking beyond his time at the bank. He wondered aloud what banking might look like 25 years from now, when BPI celebrates its 200th anniversary.
“I don’t think any of us can predict exactly what banking will look like by then,” he said.
Yet he was clear on one unfinished job: “Millions of Filipinos still have limited access to formal financial services.”

blocks.caption: GALA. BPI president and CEO TG Limcaoco (right) looks on as BPI chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala congratulates writer Roel Landingin. BPI

blocks.text: But Limcaoco isn’t always dressed up to the nines. A rather different side of him was on display two months earlier, on August 1, BPI’s actual birthday, when the bank launched a Disney-themed savings account for children.

After a morning of golf, Limcaoco, a grandfather himself, was at Glorietta — an Ayala mall, of course — talking to children about setting aside part of their allowance. As he often does, he brought the idea down to their level. Compound interest might mean little to a child, but saving for a bicycle or a dog was easy enough to understand.
“Maybe a kid puts P100 a month,” he told Rappler afterward. “The magic of interest, even though it’s small, really is meaningful.”

Meanwhile Go, then still a few months away from being officially announced as his successor, took the chance to tease her boss, joking during her remarks about whether the children should call him “Lolo TG.”
For that morning, at least, the man running one of the country’s biggest banks was simply Lolo TG, talking to kids about what they could do for their future. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Angara calls for stricter digital protection for students
articles.summary: Department of Education Secretary Sonny Angara urged technology and social media firms to implement tougher age-verification controls and delete online content that highlights violence and targets…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 1:56pm

Department of Education Secretary Sonny Angara urged technology and social media firms to implement tougher age-verification controls and delete online content that highlights violence and targets young learners into radicalization.

"We agree that we need stronger safeguards against these terrorist recruitment groups, online groomers. We need to protect our children online, and we really need stricter firewalls, not systems where a child who isn’t even in high school can just click that they are 18 years old. That cannot be allowed,” Angara said at a multisectoral forum on preventing nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) held at the University of Asia and the Pacific (UA&P).
Angara said the call came amid President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to all government agencies to seek lasting solutions to the complex issue of school violence.

Following Marcos’ orders, the Department of Education (DepEd) has created a task force with the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) child protection units to track emerging risks.

The education secretary lauded the government agencies and international and local partners for their solidarity in dealing with school safety and digital threats, adding that a number of social media companies have reached out to DepEd for discussions about enhancing safeguards in online spaces.
To combat both online and physical threats, Angara said the agency has enhanced school, learner support, and emergency response systems.
Angara said the DepEd has also partnered with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to deploy barangay officials to support campus security and police visibility.

"We must remember that while we actively stand guard and protect our children in the physical world, we also need to do the same online. We need to build stronger communities and better relationships with our learners," he said.
In line with the efforts, DepEd has expanded the Kaagapay Program to guide parents in protecting children online alongside promoting mental health awareness and identifying red flags on bullying.

Further, the agency underscored peer support through the My Buddy System and empowered school clubs, organizations, scouting and sports to provide learners positive spaces to participate. --VAL, GMA News

articles.title: 2 foreign fugitives nabbed over alleged links to large-scale fraud, illegal gambling ops
articles.summary: The Bureau of Immigration arrested two fugitives, a Taiwanese and a South Korean, in separate operations for their alleged involvement in large-scale fraud and illegal gambling operations.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 1:51pm
The Bureau of Immigration (BI) arrested two fugitives, a Taiwanese and a South Korean, in separate operations for their alleged involvement in large-scale fraud and illegal gambling operations.

In a press release issued Saturday, the BI identified the Taiwanese fugitive as Yu Sheng Fu, 27, who was apprehended in Barangay Cabancalan, Mandaue City on October 29 following a request from the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office.

“According to Taiwan’s Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB), Yu allegedly leads a fraud syndicate operating in Manila that victimized more than 200 Taiwanese nationals and defrauded them of over P200 million,” the BI added.

Meanwhile, South Korean Ha Jonhoo, 46, was arrested at the Newport Complex in Pasay City on November 2. He was wanted by South Korean authorities for his alleged involvement in an illegal online gambling operation.
The bureau said Ha reportedly acted as a junket agent who facilitated remote baccarat gambling for Korean clients from June 2019 to December 2020.
“The operation allegedly involved 37 transactions amounting to approximately 154 million South Korean won, or US$114,000,” the bureau added.
BI said both fugitives are presently detained at its detention facility in Taguig City, awaiting deportation proceedings.
After deportation orders are issued, the bureau said both will be blacklisted, barring their return to the Philippines.

BI Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said these arrests show the agency’s efforts to prevent the country from becoming a refuge from justice, noting the bureau's continued vigilance to ensure observance of the law.

“These arrests demonstrate that international borders will not shield fugitives from accountability. The Bureau remains vigilant in tracking down foreign nationals wanted for serious offenses and ensuring that those who violate our immigration laws face the appropriate legal consequences,” Viado said.
“We will continue to act decisively while observing due process and the rule of law,” he added. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/KG, GMA News

articles.summary: A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Democrats took control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, making extraordinary gains deep in Republican territory with voters delivering a sharp rebuke to President Donald Trump and his agenda.

A wave of anger over Trump’s policies, particularly the US-Iran war’s role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives.

Donald Trump’s party has been defeated in states where it hadn’t lost for a generation — or longer: Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. These have been red states for quite some time, but this shows the Republicans really suffered in their own heartland.
Meanwhile, Malacanang announced on November 5 that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has chosen Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as the country’s 28th Supreme Court chief justice.

Zalameda, the third most senior among the chief justice nominees, replaces Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo who retired during the weekend. Zalameda will serve as chief justice for seven years or until August 2033, when he reaches the mandatory retirement age of 70.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: SC didn’t rule Marcos’ budget signing unconstitutional
articles.summary: The Court faulted Congress for raising the President's proposed budget, and with the decision not yet final, no formal probe has been opened

blocks.text: The Court faulted Congress for raising the President's proposed budget, and with the decision not yet final, no formal probe has been opened

items: The Supreme Court ruled that the national budgets for 2024 and 2025 were unconstitutional due to Congress adding excessive funds, not because of President Marcos's signature.
The ruling is not yet final, as the Office of the Solicitor General has filed a motion for clarification and reconsideration regarding the budget's legality.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Claim: The Supreme Court (SC) ruled that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s signing of the national budget was unconstitutional.

Why we fact-checked this: A graphic shared by the Facebook page Makata Ng Bayan on November 1 shows an edited photo of Marcos, former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo, and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla.

The text on the graphic reads: “Sinabi na ng Supreme Court na Unconstitutional ang Pagpirma ni Marcos sa Budget! Tungkulin ng Ombudsman, DOJ at COA mag Imbestiga, Pero bakit di nila ginawa? Mga Duwag ba sila o Mukhang Pera?”

(The Supreme Court has already said Marcos’s signing of the budget was unconstitutional! It’s the duty of the Ombudsman, Department of Justice (DOJ), and Commission on Audit (COA) to investigate, but why didn’t they? Are they cowards or money-hungry?)
At the time of writing, the post had 4,900 reactions, 1,200 comments, and 2,400 shares.
The facts: The SC did declare national budgets unconstitutional, but because of what Congress added to them, not because of the President’s signature.

In a ruling released on October 20, written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the Court voted 13-2 to strike down the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, along with two rules in this year’s budget on how standby funds can be released.

The Court said Congress is not allowed to make the budget bigger than what the President proposed. In 2024, lawmakers added P449.5 billion in standby funds to the budget, and P17.99 billion more for the 2025 DPWH Special Road Fund. (READ: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations)
Not yet final: Court spokesperson Camille Ting said the ruling is not yet final, and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) could file a motion for reconsideration within 15 days from notice.

The OSG has since filed a motion for clarification and partial reconsideration, signed by Solicitor General Darlene Berberabe. The motion asks the Court to spell out which projects already funded under the budgets can continue, and to declare that the 2025 Special Road Fund increase was constitutional.

It also asked the Court not to count standby funds under the same spending limit as the rest of the budget, and to treat its new rules on releasing those funds as guidance rather than binding requirements.
No ongoing investigations: As of writing, the Ombudsman, DOJ, and COA have not opened a formal probe. The Ombudsman is also waiting for the SC’s final decision.
In 2025, it temporarily put on hold a graft complaint against House leaders over the 2025 budget until the Court resolved the constitutional question with finality.

The Court said officials behind the budget increases could still face criminal, civil, or administrative cases, unless the proper court or body finds they acted in good faith. On October 26, Remulla announced a “budget watch” and said he would form a team to study the decision and determine who may be held liable.

Vice President Sara Duterte said Marcos and Congress should answer for approving the budgets, while Malacañang said it disagreed with parts of the ruling. Senator Panfilo Lacson and Representative Leila de Lima welcomed the decision as a win for accountability. – Jake Gomez/Rappler.com

blocks.text: LEADER. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva speaks as he attends a meeting of the National Council for Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE), at the Planalto Palace in Brasilia, Brazil, on November 5, 2026.
Diego Herculano/Reuters
Just weeks after a historic election triumph, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will head to the Philippines to join global leaders at the 49th ASEAN Summit

items: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will attend the 49th ASEAN Summit in the Philippines as a guest of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Lula, who recently won a historic fourth term, will participate in the summit alongside other global leaders from November 15 to 18, after attending the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey.
His fourth term may be challenging due to the election of a conservative Congress in Brazil, following his previous imprisonment on corruption charges that were later overturned.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to the Philippines to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, just over two weeks after winning an unprecedented fourth term.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed Lula’s attendance on Friday, November 6, noting he was invited as a guest of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
“Brazil was invited as Guest of the Chair,” said ASEAN spokesperson Dax Imperial.
Lula will join other global leaders, including US President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres in the main summit from November 15 to 18.
Prior to arriving in the Philippines on November 13, Lula is expected to be in Antalya, Turkey, for the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) from November 11 to 12.
Just a few weeks ago, the 81-year-old Lula pulled off a shock election victory over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, won a historic fourth term in a stunning October 25 result that defied polls and marked another comeback in his career.
Last August, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro met with Lula to reinforce bilateral ties as the Philippines and Brazil celebrated their 80th diplomatic anniversary.
Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century.
He was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
Lula’s fourth term, though, could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. – with a report from Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
articles.summary:
Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress

It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025…

blocks.text: It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.

blocks.caption: André Corrêa do Lago, Cop30 president, sits as Simon Stiell, UN climate chief, left, speaks with other officials at Cop30 in Belém. The summit in Brazil ended with a deal that few loved. Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.
There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.

blocks.caption: An oil spill at Lake Maracaibo in Bachaquero, Venezuela. Crude oil leaks devastate fishing communities, coat wildlife and cause severe ecological degradation around the lake. Photograph: Henry Chirinos/EPA

blocks.text: The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.
Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with security forces in an attempt to storm the Cop30 headquarters in Belém in 2025. Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPA

blocks.text: Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”
A messy compromise

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.

Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.

The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Student List celebrate winning Serbia’s election last month. The defeat of authoritarian rulers is seen as a positive sign by climate campaigners. Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters

blocks.text: Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.
Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.

“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”
While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.

“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”

blocks.caption: A search and rescue operation in mudslide-hit Gyirong county in Tibet. The disaster in August was triggered by a glacier collapse. Photograph: Xinhua/AP

blocks.text: Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.

“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”

And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.

Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.

Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.

blocks.caption: Solar panels hang on a shop facade in Karachi. The technology provides a quarter of Pakistan’s electricity. Photograph: Asim Hafeez/Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”

Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.
That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”

After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.

blocks.caption: Preparations for Cop31 are under way in Antalya, Turkey. Australia is co-host of the event. Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.

However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.

“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.
“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”
People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.
“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

articles.title: Eya Laure takes charge amid Choco Mucho’s PVL meltdowns
articles.summary: Choco Mucho star Eya Laure keeps a long-term outlook as the Flying Titans fall prey to a pair of huge collapses to kickstart their 2026 PVL All-Filipino Conference title push

blocks.text: READY. Eya Laure accepts Choco Mucho's leadership challenge.
PVL
Choco Mucho star Eya Laure keeps a long-term outlook as the Flying Titans fall prey to a pair of huge collapses to kickstart their 2026 PVL All-Filipino Conference title push

items: The Choco Mucho Flying Titans, a prominent team in the PVL, have struggled to maintain success in recent tournaments despite a decent early record.
Key players Eya Laure and Sisi Rondina-Rosales have performed well, but the team has faced challenges, including significant losses and a lack of energy from other members.
With a focus on teamwork and perseverance, the Titans aim to improve and reclaim their position in the league, despite setbacks and competition from other strong teams.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – As one of the most popular and strongest teams in the PVL, the Choco Mucho Flying Titans have always been held to a higher standard than others with each passing conference.
Unfortunately, while fans have always turned out for Choco Mucho, the success has not really followed in recent tournaments, including the current All-Filipino tilt.
On paper, an early 3-2 record is decent, but the way the Flying Titans gave up those two losses quickly revealed a somewhat troubling side of the two-time PVL silver medalists.

Last October 22, Farm Fresh dug itself out of a 2-0 match hole to hand Choco Mucho a stunning 20-25, 26-28, 25-23, 25-23, 15-13 reverse sweep, before the Titans rebounded with a four-set victory over winless Galeries Tower just five days later.

However, just as it was on pace to restart a winning streak, Choco Mucho again collapsed, this time in four sets to undefeated Nxled, largely thanks to a massive third-set turnaround that saw the Chameleons bury the Titans with an 11-1 scoring spree to overcome a 22-14 deficit.

In times like these, Choco Mucho star Eya Laure reminds herself that each conference is a constant test of leadership, that true contenders cannot let up nor let themselves be overcome by negative emotions, especially when under pressure from other aspiring contenders.

“I think it’s more in our mindset that we are the ones who have to work harder for one another — that we play for each other, for the team, for the coaches, for [mother company] Rebisco,” Laure said in Filipino after the demoralizing defeat last Tuesday, November 3.

Though Laure and longtime teammate Sisi Rondina-Rosales were excellent as usual with 18 and 14 points apiece, but the rest of the Titans were unable to keep the energy up for their leaders, which was especially telling as Nxled staged a 25-17 fourth-set blowout to seal the win.

For the rest of the conference and the season, it is up to leaders like Laure and Rondina-Rosales to remind the rest of the squad that consistent success is the product of a long process, and that it will all come apart if they stop believing now.

“Whatever the results may be, we will go through this together, and we will learn together in these kinds of games,” Laure continued. “Most of us are just approaching one year with Choco Mucho and are fairly new to the team.”

“We are just here to build whatever we can still give to Choco Mucho in this conference. We’ll do our best, and wherever we end up eventually, we’ll accept that first. We’ll take the wins that we can get, and we’ll work harder from that point.”

Following its back-to-back conference runner-up finishes across 2023 and 2024, Choco Mucho has yet to return to the PVL podium — finishing no higher than fifth place in the five tournaments that have since passed.

Though national team-related absences to the likes of Laure and Rondina and the ever-present scourge of injuries have hampered Choco Mucho’s path to consistent contention, the pieces are certainly in place for a real push for the championship.

While many teams have since consolidated absurd levels of talent from multiple high-profile team disbandments and hiatuses, the Flying Titans are still in the upper echelon of the league in terms of ability and star power.
They just have to believe again that they belong. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments
articles.summary: The US urged Beijing to meet commitments from a 2025 accord — particularly on agricultural purchases and rare earths supply. China, meanwhile, expressed concern over the US' "economic, trade…

image.caption: The US call comes ahead of a scheduled meeting between Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping later this month [FILE: Sept 23, 2026]Image: Al Drago/CNP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Top officials of United States President Donald Trump's administration have called on China to "fully and immediately" implement its commitments under a 2025 trade agreement between the two nations, including on rare earth and other critical minerals.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Friday held a videoconference with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the trade and economic relationship between Washington and Beijing, a statement from Greer's office said.

Greer "emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals.” it added.
The US-China trade agreement

The US officials were referring to an accord reached between the world's two largest economies in 2025 in a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in South Korea's Busan, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
The deal had been reached during a period that saw the two countries exchange tariff escalations prompted by Trump's wider tariffs policy, which particularly targeted China, among other countries.
The accord capped US tariffs on Chinese goods — enforced during Trump's second stint as president — at about 20%.
China agreed to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans for the next three years.
Beijing also said it would keep China's rare earth exports flowing, suspending new export curbs.
The minerals are critical for the technological industry, and the Trump administration has in the past complained that Beijing was not meeting its commitments regarding supply.

"The Trump Administration will continue pursuing policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen our economic and national security,” Bessent wrote on X after the high-level call.
China raises concern over US trade restrictions

He, who is Beijing's lead negotiator on trade ties with the US, during Friday's interaction expressed "serious concern" over recent US trade restrictions targeting his country, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
The report did not elaborate which measure the vice premier was referring to.
But both parties agreed to "continuously strengthen cooperation”and "properly manage differences" to promote a "stable" US-China trade relationship, Xinhua said.
The Busan trade deal at first covered only one year, but the US and China extended their trade pact until January 10 next year, as Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September.
The two leaders are expected to meet again at the upcoming APEC forum in Shenzhen, China, slated from November 18 to 19.

Meanwhile, in a separate development, China has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic trilateral summit of Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC gathering.

China "is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, said at a media briefing in Beijing this week.

articles.title: BIR 'data leak' under gov't probe
articles.summary: The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is working with the Department of Information and Communication Technology (DICT) and anti-cybercrime law enforcement units to investigate an alleged leak of its…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 12:27pm

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is working with the Department of Information and Communication Technology (DICT) and anti-cybercrime law enforcement units to investigate an alleged leak of its agency data.

In an advisory, the BIR said it is conducting the probe and beefing up security measures in coordination with the DICT and the latter's attached agencies, the National Computer Emergency Response Team (NCERT) and Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC).
It is also working with the Philippine National Police (PNP) Anti-Cybercrime Group regarding the incident, which supposedly occurred on Friday, November 7.
"The Bureau of Internal Revenue is aware of reports circulating online... regarding an alleged leak involving data claimed to be associated with the agency," the advisory read.
The taxman did not provide details about the potential extent of the data leak, or the type of information which may have been reportedly compromised.
"We wish to inform the public that these claims are being treated with utmost urgency and priority," it added.
On September 8, the BIR website suffered what the bureau described as a "brief defacement incident."
Technical teams from the BIR and DICT were able to promptly restore website services.

"Based on the BIR's initial assessment, taxpayer information and core BIR systems were not affected by the incident. As a precaution, the BIR is conducting additional security checks," the bureau said at the time.
The reported BIR data "leak" on Friday comes just over a week after private healthcare provider St. Luke's Medical Center was hit by a "cybersecurity incident" on its mobile application.

The National Privacy Commission (NPC) is currently investigating the matter, which said it received a "data breach notification" from St. Luke's. The commission said some 100,000 people may have been affected.

Although it assured that its critical Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system containing patient records was not compromised, St. Luke's also started reaching out to individuals whose personal information may have been affected.
Last June, the DICT said it was investigating a reported hack of the House of Representatives website, which was allegedly defaced.
Shortly thereafter, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said it has identified persons behind the hacking of several government websites. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: North Korea’s army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
articles.summary: The lifestyle of a hacker or elite technology worker for North Korea is grueling. PSCORE executive director Nam Bada says, 'There is always pressure to keep earning money.'

items: North Korea's cyber operations have evolved significantly, with hackers trained in advanced technologies and tasked with high-stakes cyber heists, including the recent $6.3 billion Binance hack.

Despite the grueling working conditions and constant pressure, North Korean hackers are seen as a strategic asset for the regime, with state backing allowing them to operate with little fear of consequences.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

North Korea rewards its top hackers, tasked with heists like the Binance crypto hack that netted a cool $6.3 billion, with perks such as a spacious apartment in the capital of Pyongyang and huge hard currency awards.

Leader Kim Jong Un has assembled an army of world-class hackers using such incentives in a program more than a decade old that picks 200 of the smartest middle school students each year to study computer engineering, defectors and analysts say.
A fraction eventually become hackers in a group that has evolved from running illegal gambling websites in the early days to pulling off the world’s biggest cyber heist last month, they say.

blocks.caption: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3-billion security breach

blocks.text: “They are actually one of Kim Jong Un’s secret weapons,” said Kim Heung-kwang, a North Korean defector who trained hackers on behalf of the state before fleeing to South Korea in 2004.

“There is no other country grooming hackers like this, systematically searching for the smartest children, solely to turn them into operatives,” he added. “Whether they want to be a hacker or not does not matter.”

The FBI and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”.
The denial is part of a pattern in which the North dismisses such blame over the years as fabricated political provocations.

North Korea set up a cyber unit in 1998 but elevated its status after Kim came to power and declared in 2013 that cyber warfare was, along with nuclear weapons and missiles, an “all purpose sword” crucial to the country’s strike capability.

Candidate selection begins in middle school as early as 11 or 12 years of age, with authorities picking about 150 to 200 children a year to study computer science, said Kim Heung-kwang, the former trainer, and two defectors who worked in IT.
At 17, the top performers are sent to North Korea’s best universities and undergo further screening before a chosen few finally enter the military’s cyber unit as hackers, they added.

They are trained in areas such as cryptocurrency protocols and reverse-engineering foreign hardware devices in addition to more conventional topics such as advanced mathematics and foreign languages, one of them said.
Those who do not become hackers are trained to turn out software or apps for Western firms via remote jobs.

“While South Korea’s best students may pursue medicine or other prestigious careers, North Korea channels top talent into nuclear and cyber programs and essentially guarantees their future,” said Lim Jongin, professor emeritus at the school of cybersecurity at Korea University.
Other privileges on tap for the hackers are travel abroad to allied countries, such as China, where they can more freely access the internet.

Successful exploits can earn as much as 30% of the heist’s profits in US dollars for the hackers’ military unit, and they can even receive a flat in the capital where their parents can also stay, Kim said.
“There are accounts that successful cyber personnel are given apartments in Pyongyang,” Lim said, adding that the flats could range to as much as 132 sq m (1,420 sq ft).
Such performers are also eligible for membership of the ruling party and high-status marriages into elite families, said one of the defectors.
But it is a small group. The North’s cyberwarfare operations employ about 8,400 people, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated in 2024.
North Korean state media do not publicly celebrate such hackers’ achievements, but they regularly highlight students who show talent for programming.
In 2015, North Korea opened the Mirae Scientists Street in the capital, in the construction of which Kim Jong Un had been closely involved, state media said.
Hackers’ formal designation in the North was “scientist” or “researcher”, said one of the defectors.

Other hacking groups associated with North Korea include the Lazarus Group, also known as APT38, which the US accused in 2022 of having stolen hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency from the Ronin blockchain network. The FBI has said TraderTraitor is affiliated to Lazarus.
State backing makes the North’s hackers more dangerous and harder to repulse, as they face no consequences for hack after hack, enabling them to perfect their strategies, analysts said.
“In the world of cyber crime, often, if you make a mistake … that is all law enforcement needs to get you,” said Alec Zebrick, senior manager for Asia-Pacific global services at Chainalysis.
But North Korea’s hackers “are doing this for the regime, so they’re going to continue, even after successes,” he added.
“Even after failures, they’ll continue, because it’s very hard for the international community to take action against them.”

Other groups that have engaged with North Korea IT workers who earn funds for the Kim regime by landing remote technology jobs at Western companies describe them as highly organised, polite in their interactions and avid users of AI.

“There clearly was a structure you would see in military. Strict times, cleaning boots, very orderly,” said YouTuber Deeveeaar, who has claimed to have hacked into cameras watching North Korean IT workers at their jobs.
“To say they ‘use a lot of AI’ is an understatement. AI is the very backbone of their operation,” he said, citing use of paid ChatGPT accounts, Claude Code and Cursor, among many AI tools.
“They write code with it, alter their resumes and help make new ones. And even forge documents and identities.”
Binance said the hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise staffers’ computers before using an internal AI tool to seize control of systems.
In 2025, a sanctions monitoring team drawn from 11 United Nations members said TraderTraitor had obtained both ChatGPT and DeepSeek accounts.
Yet the lifestyle of a hacker or elite technology worker for North Korea is grueling, particularly when given a mission or sent abroad, say former IT workers and human rights groups.

Living in cramped spaces, often working stretches longer than 10 hours a day, constant surveillance and strict targets are among the downsides, said former IT workers interviewed for a report last year by advocacy group PSCORE.

“There is always pressure to keep earning money,” said the group’s executive director, Nam Bada. “The stress is extreme, and because of the psychological strain people develop health problems they didn’t have before.”
IT workers must meet a monthly target in dollars, or face humiliation and other punishments, he said.
Still, the hackers’ success is likely to embolden the North Korean leader as they get better and grow more ambitious, analysts say.
“We see more and more of them leaning towards what we call ‘big game hunting’,” said Zebrick.
“So they’re targeting some of these larger organizations, potentially have larger vaults of funds, that they could potentially get. These are harder targets,” he added.
“However, as we can see with the Binance case, the payout certainly can make it worth their time.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.

blocks.text: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.
