articles.title: Cornell faculty declares 'no confidence' in university leadership
articles.summary: The university leadership has faced intense criticism for its handling of sexual crimes on campus since a former student filed a lawsuit saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in…

image.caption: Cornell is trying to mend its reputation following its handling of a sexual assault case in 2024 [FILE: Sept 28, 2026]Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring "no confidence" in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis on campus.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
What's behind the resolution?

The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.

The university leadership has faced intense criticism since mid-September when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved.

blocks.caption: The university's handling of the Jane Doe case sparked protests across the USImage: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.

The allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was later met with widespread criticism.
The investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.
What did the board chair say about the faculty vote?

Some faculty members have criticized University President Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.

The faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders but the resolution's backers had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
After the faculty vote, Cornell Board Chair Anne Smalling said it "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable."
But she also expressed the board of trustees' support for President Kotlikoff and the administration.
"We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again."
Resolution 'only the beginning'
Kotlikoff ​has yet to respond to the outcome of the faculty vote.
Under university procedures, the president has 30 days to respond in writing, a university spokesperson said.
Kotlikoff said the day before voting began on October 29 that faculty discussion and debate were "an important component of ⁠Cornell's ​shared governance."

He also pointed out that the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil ​rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.
Iris Packman, a co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, told the Associated Press on Friday that the vote was "only the beginning" and that faculty would push for sweeping reforms.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell junior who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution's sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university's response.

"We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged," she said. "It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell."

articles.title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
articles.summary:
The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated

Donald Trump has said the US military…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.
In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump speaks to reporters on arrival at Palm Beach, Florida. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters

blocks.text: Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.
Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.
“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.
The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.
The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.
With the Associated Press

articles.title: This activist lives the real-world struggle of ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’
articles.summary: Acquitted after five years in prison, activist Amanda Echanis shows that the human rights message of the award-winning documentary ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’ doesn't stop when the film ends

blocks.text: For 38-year-old peasant organizer Amanda Echanis, activism is both a personal calling and an inherited legacy. As a leader for the Cagayan provincial chapter of AMIHAN, she carries a deep history of resisting injustice — a fight woven into her family bloodline.

Echanis’ life and struggle are central to Noni Abao’s documentary Bloom Where You Are Planted, alongside fellow activists Agnes Mesina and the late Randy Malayao. The powerful film, which chronicles state repression and land rights in the Cagayan Valley, recently swept the 49th Gawad Urian Awards, taking home four major trophies: Best Film, Best Documentary, Best Direction, and Best Editing.

On December 2, 2020, state forces raided Echanis’ home in Baggao, Cagayan, arresting her on trumped-up charges of illegal possession of firearms and explosives. She was sent to prison alongside her then-one-month-old infant son, Randall Emmanuel.

Her quest for justice faced repeated pre-trial delays, extending her detention to over five years. Finally, on January 14, 2026, the Tuguegarao City Regional Trial Court Branch 10 acquitted Echanis after the prosecution failed to prove her guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

“Masaya na malaya na ako, kasama ang aking anak, matapos mapawalang-sala sa mga gawa-gawang paratang na ipinapataw sa mga katulad kong aktibista at artista ng bayan,” Echanis shared through PanitikanPH, a project of the UP Institute of Creative Writing.
(I’m happy that I’m free, with my son, after my acquittal from the fabricated charges imposed on activists and artists like me.)

“Narito sa aking patuloy na pagkilos, patuloy na paglikha, patuloy na paglilingkod sa kapwa lalo na sa mga batayang sektor sa lipunan at lalo na sa patuloy na pagsusulat — dito ko nahahanap ang aking paghinga, sa ideya na nagpapatuloy ako at hindi kailanman humupa sa pagkilos sa kabila ng pagkakapiit.”

(It’s through my continued action, my ongoing creation, my persistent service to others — especially to the marginalized sectors of society — and especially through my constant writing, that I find my breathing space. I will never back down despite the imprisonment.)

Echanis inherited her fierce commitment to social justice from her parents. Her father, prominent peasant leader and peace consultant Randall Echanis, was brutally murdered in his Manila home in August 2020.
Through the human rights organization Karapatan, Amanda continues to urge the public to hold the government accountable for her father’s unsolved killing.

Her mother, Linda Echanis, has long stood in solidarity with the movement. In a striking historical parallel, Amanda was first detained with her parents when she was just two years old following her father’s arrest on identical fabricated charges — making her the country’s youngest political prisoner at the time.
Additionally, her lineage extends to her uncle, Emmanuel Lacaba, a renowned activist-poet who joined the New People’s Army and was killed in South Cotabato in 1976.
An artist who uses literature as a weapon for advocacy, Echanis graduated from the Philippine High School for the Arts.

While in prison, she re-enrolled remotely at the University of the Philippines Diliman to finish her degree in Creative Writing. Making history in May 2025, she became the first political prisoner to run for and win a seat on the UP Diliman Student Council, topping the councilor race via remote video campaign calls.

As a writer, her published works focus heavily on land reform, human rights, and social justice. Her notable pieces include Nanay Mameng, a stage play depicting urban poverty through the eyes of an 86-year-old activist, Tatlong Paslit na Alaala, and her prison poetry collection, Binhi ng Paglaya.

In Bloom Where You Are Planted, the audience hears a moving recording of Echanis reading a poem about her parents’ activism, alongside a poignant clip of her assuring her son that “this, too, shall pass.”
Reflecting on the documentary’s success, Echanis stresses that its relevance is far from over.
“Ang pinaka-memorable na part ng pagpapalabas ng ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’ ay hindi ito nagtatapos na kasaysayan,” she told Rappler.
“Ito ay nagpapatuloy pa rin hanggang sa kasalukuyan ang mga pagpapalabas ng pelikula sa iba’t ibang mga unibersidad, mga pagawaan, at mga sakahan, at kung nasaan ang mga simpleng mga mamamayan.”

(The most memorable part of Bloom Where You Are Planted is that it is not finished history. Film screenings continue to this day in various universities, workplaces, and farms — wherever the ordinary citizens are.)
With the youth making up a massive portion of today’s advocates, Echanis actively encourages them to use their creativity to amplify vulnerable sectors.
“‘Wag tayong matakot na alamin ang mga nangyayari sa lipunan, na paglingkuran ‘yung mga pinakamahihirap na sektor sa ating bansa — ang mga magsasaka,“ she said.
(Don’t be afraid to know what is happening in society. And don’t be afraid to serve the poorest sectors of our country — the farmers.) – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

items: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested for possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs with underage girls, found in storage units in California.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, was arrested on Friday, November 6, on a charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs of himself with naked underage girls, found in rented storage units in California.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was taken into custody by federal agents in Florida, where according to the Daily Mail the elder Markle, who uses a wheelchair, was a nursing home patient.
“Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions,” Patel said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Meghan Markle sends letter to father hospitalized in the Philippines

blocks.text: In a criminal complaint filed on Thursday, November 5, in US District Court in Los Angeles, Markle was charged with one count of “possession of child pornography.”
If convicted, Markle could face up to 20 years in prison, the Justice Department said.
Markle, a resident of Lakeland, Florida, made his initial court appearance before a US magistrate judge in nearby Tampa.
The judge ordered him released to await trial on condition that he submit to home detention and electronic monitoring, the US Attorney’s Office in Los Angeles said in a statement.
No plea was entered, and an arraignment is not expected for several weeks, according to the statement.
Markle’s defense counsel was not immediately known, and it was not clear when he might be transferred to California to face the charge against him.

According to an FBI affidavit filed as part of the criminal complaint, Markle kept the sexually explicit material in question in two Los Angeles-area storage units he has rented since 2008, which agents searched last week after obtaining a warrant.
Agents seized approximately 78 items, including slides, 35mm film negatives, and books containing child sexual abuse images, according to the affidavit.

The 13-page document stated that at least two of the frames on film negatives showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a “nude pre-pubescent girl” in poses “designed to elicit a sexual response in the viewer.” In one image, the man appeared to be fondling the girl’s genitalia.
Buckingham Palace and a spokesperson for Meghan Markle did not respond to requests for comment.
Authorities in the Philippines, where Thomas Markle had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse images.

British police last month said they would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that claims had not been passed to other authorities when they were first received.

The FBI began its investigation of Markle in October, according to its affidavit, after hearing from a witness who said they had discovered suspected child abuse material among Markle’s possessions in the Philippines.
The FBI also spoke last month with a second witness, also unidentified in the affidavit, who said Markle rented at least one storage unit in California.
At least one of the photographs reviewed by the FBI shows Markle was staying at a hotel or motel in the Philippines, based on the logo seen on the pillows on the bed.
Markle denied the accusations of possessing child sexual abuse material when they initially came to light, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies.”
Meghan Markle, an American actor who married King Charles’ younger son in 2018, has said she was “deeply distressed” over the allegations. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Prosecution had its chance. It failed': Duterte camp says ahead of VP Sara's defense
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's camp hit back at the impeachment prosecution, accusing its members of disregarding due process and using public briefings to push allegations against her ahead of the…

blocks.text: Headlines
November 7, 2026 | 10:05am
In this photo uploaded on Facebook on Oct. 26, 2026 shows Vice President Sara Duterte during the World Teachers' Day celebration at the SMX Convention Center in Lanang, Davao City.
Sara Duterte via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte's camp hit back at the impeachment prosecution, accusing its members of disregarding due process and using public briefings to push allegations against her ahead of the start of her defense on Monday, November 9.

"The prosecution had its chance. It failed. On Monday, the Vice President begins her defense," spokesperson Salvador Paolo A. Panelo Jr. said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday, November 7.
Panelo said allegations against Duterte should be proven in court through clear and convincing evidence, adding that an accused should not be condemned before being heard.

He also took aim at private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan and her colleagues, accusing them of trying to sway public opinion through what he described as "asinine sound bites built on half-truths and malicious speculation."
The statement came a day after Kapunan said Duterte could become the prosecution's strongest evidence if she takes the witness stand.
Kapunan made the remark when asked whether the vice president's appearance before the impeachment court would allow her to address allegations of amassing around P817 million in unexplained wealth.
"If the Vice President appears before the impeachment court, she will be the best evidence against herself due to her demeanor, the way she answers," Kapunan said.
She also questioned whether Duterte would take an oath to tell the truth, citing her refusal to do so during previous House hearings.

Kapunan pointed to Duterte's statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALNs), which listed her interests in Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and GenCorp. Foods Industries Inc. She also questioned the absence of declared cash on hand or in bank accounts in the vice president's SALNs from 2019 to 2025, despite bank officials' testimonies about her deposits.

The prosecutor also cited P776 million in remittances sent to Cale88 Foods Corp., a banana chips company listed as an asset in the SALN of Duterte's husband. She said the amount was not reflected in the couple's joint SALN.
Duterte's defense team has submitted an initial list of at least 24 witnesses it intends to present during the trial.

Former University of St. La Salle College of Law dean Ralph Sarmiento, who was supposed to be the defense's first witness, has since declined the invitation. He said he wanted to preserve the independence of his constitutional law scholarship and legal views.

The defense said Sarmiento was expected to testify on constitutional principles relevant to Article II of the impeachment complaint, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth, SALN discrepancies and failure to divest from business interests.
Hearings resume at 10 a.m. on Monday, November 9, with sessions also set for November 10 to 13, 19, 20 and 23.

articles.title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts
articles.summary:
Santiago Peña was detained minutes after he was impeached by Congress, as protesters took to the streets demanding answers after the suspension of the Ueno bank

Paraguay’s rightwing…

blocks.text: Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts.

Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities.

The move froze the accounts of 2.9 million people, about 60% of the country’s adult population, who were customers of the bank – Ueno - and who overnight could no longer use their own money even for basic purchases such as bread and water.
Protests spread across the country, some involving violent clashes with police. Impeachment proceedings began on Wednesday before being concluded on Friday, minutes before Peña’s arrest was ordered.

His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, was being sworn in as the country’s new leader while a public prosecutor, accompanied by police outside Peña’s home, told local media the former president had been placed under house arrest.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators take part in a protest against the banking crisis. Photograph: Jose Bogado/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “It has been established that he is indeed inside his home. He voluntarily allowed officers to enter and made himself available for all procedural purposes,” said prosecutor Elena Fiore Franco.
The public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into Peña on Thursday on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling.

Peña, who was one of US president Donald Trump’s main allies in the region, had tried to resign on Thursday in an attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who become senators for life in Paraguay – but lawmakers did not accept his resignation, leaving him subject to the ordinary courts.

Amid rumours he had fled to Argentina, the 47-year-old economist was expected to appear before Congress to present his defence during the impeachment proceedings, but left that to his lawyers and instead continued posting on social media.

blocks.caption: A file photo of Paraguay’s impeached president Santiago Peña. Photograph: César Olmedo/Reuters

blocks.text: Before the impeachment was concluded or the arrest warrant issued, he posted: “I say goodbye with gratitude, while fully recognising the anguish of those who are now waiting for answers,” referring to former Ueno customers who are unable to access their own money.

Soon after taking office, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, a former CEO of Ueno, head of the country’s central bank. Three months later, Spalding – who was by now regulating the company he used to run – allowed Ueno to become a digital bank, which put it on the path to becoming one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years.
The arrest warrant for Peña also includes Spalding.

Peña himself had about US$1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.

blocks.caption: Pedro Alliana is sworn in as president of Paraguay on Friday. Photograph: Nathalia Aguilar/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: As the bank aggressively expanded through an easy account-opening system and by promising returns far above those offered by the rest of the market, it also managed to bring public pension funds controlled by Peña’s administration into its portfolio.

“Because Ueno had the blessing of the presidency, most of the pension funds close to the government went to deposit their money in the bank,” said political analyst Hugo Duarte. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.
As pressure mounted and retail sales fell by as much as 80% because much of the population could not access their own money, Peña lost the support of his own party.

During the impeachment session, opposition senator Rafael Filizzola said Paraguay was facing “one of the biggest corruption scandals since the return of democracy” and the “biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era”.

articles.title: Cornell faculty vote no confidence in university's leadership
articles.summary: The faculty senate of Cornell University approved a resolution Friday declaring no confidence in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a…

image.caption: A person holds a fist in the air during a protest over sexual assault allegations at Cornell University on Oct. 8. (David Ryder/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The faculty senate of Cornell University approved a resolution Friday declaring no confidence in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
Advocates hope symbolic vote will pressure school to address longstanding institutional failures
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to senate members on Friday afternoon.

The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman's allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious Ithaca, N.Y., university.

While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.

Board of Trustees chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote "reflects the deep anger across our campus" and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to "thoughtfully and comprehensively" address the issue.

Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, expressed hope in a statement that "this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
Jane Doe’s home was swatted, says lawyer in Cornell gang-rape case

All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong investigation.
Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
President defends his leadership

Speaking to faculty senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.

Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell's reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman's case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.
A Cornell University banner hangs in Willard Straight Hall during a town hall meeting about the university’s handling of the case, in Ithaca, N.Y. on Oct. 6. (Angelina Katsanis/Reuters)

Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. deputy attorney general Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine Cornell's inital response to the rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell undergrad who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution's sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university's response.

"We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged," she said. "It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell."
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation.

articles.title: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff
articles.summary: US president confirms Susie Wiles, current chief of staff and first woman to serve in the role, will step down

blocks.text: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.
The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.
In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.
Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”
“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”
Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.
In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”
She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller posted on X that he was “honored beyond words” to serve as Trump’s chief of staff. He added: “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”
But a growing chorus of Democrats condemned the appointment.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, posted: “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Chuck Schumer, likely to be the next majority leader of the Senate, wrote: “Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”
David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.
A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.
after newsletter promotion

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”
Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.
Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.
Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

Anthony Scaramucci, who had a brief spell as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Trump saw the midterm results and decided elevating Stephen Miller is the answer. 🤣 He is even more delusional than I thought. Or maybe he actually wants to finish destroying the @GOP? 🤔”

articles.title: Meghan Markle's dad arrested in US over child sex abuse images found in PH
articles.summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan Markle, was arrested in Florida on Friday over alleged possession of child sexual abuse images, some of which were reportedly found at his former home in…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 9:13am
In this screenshot, Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Duchess of Sussex Meghan, speaks in an interview with Australian morning show Sunrise in September 2021.
Sunrise on YouTube; Philstar.com screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan Markle, was arrested in Florida on Friday over alleged possession of child sexual abuse images, some of which were reportedly found at his former home in the Philippines, Agence France-Presse reported.
Markle, 82, faces one count of possession of child pornography. He is expected to appear before a court in Tampa, Florida, on Friday, US Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement.
"Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," Essayli said.
"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," he added.
FBI agents arrested Markle early Friday at the retirement home where he lives in Lakeland, Florida.

The US Department of Justice said Markle allegedly kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two storage units in the Los Angeles area that he had rented for nearly two decades.
Agents seized around 78 items from the units, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material, the department said.
Markle faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.
Images of child sexual abuse were also allegedly found at his former home in the Philippines and in a storage unit he rented in Mexico.
British tabloid The Sun reported last month that Markle's son, Thomas Markle Jr., discovered the images while going through boxes at his father's former home in the Philippines.
Markle had been living in Cebu before reportedly returning to the United States earlier this year.

Meghan said last month that she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations involving her father. She also said she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations.
Meghan married Prince Harry, the younger son of King Charles III, at Windsor Castle in May 2018.
The couple stepped back from their royal duties in 2020 and left Britain. They have since been living in the United States with their two children.

articles.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
articles.summary: Jehovah's Witness leaders relaxed strict rules on blood transfusions, but the change came 23 days too late for Isaac Valdez.

blocks.text: In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.

Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.

The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.

Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.

The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.

This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.

"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.

We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.

They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

articles.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
articles.summary: For some tourists, the contrast between Somalia's reputation and what they experience on the ground can be striking.

blocks.text: As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.

This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.

But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.

The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.

Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.

But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.

Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

articles.title: How Stephen Miller appointment shows Trump hasn’t learned his lesson on immigration
articles.summary:
US voters repudiated mass deportation campaign, but choice of new chief of staff shows Trump doesn’t care

On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation…

blocks.text: On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.
But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff.

It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states.

But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed.

Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.

blocks.caption: A person is detained by US Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) agents near a Lowe’s hardware store in New Orleans, Louisiana, on 3 December. Photograph: Adam Gray/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signals a doubling down on the administration’s cruelest impulses,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “Miller’s promotion guarantees an acceleration of mass deportations and of brute force unleashed within our neighborhoods.”

After immigration agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a nurse, amid immigration raids in Minneapolis, it was Miller, according to the Wall Street Journal, who raised the idea that Trump could invoke the Insurrection Act to send in military troops.

It was Miller who came up with the legal framework of using the Alien Enemies Act to cast Venezuelan immigrants – including asylum seekers – as foreign terrorists associated with the Tren de Aragua cartel, and using that reasoning to expel them to a Salvadorian megaprison and to strike small Venezuelan boats.

During the first Trump administration, it was Miller who devised the “Muslim ban” restricting travel from Muslim-majority countries. It was he who designed the now-notorious zero tolerance policy of the first Trump administration – which separated more than 5,600 children from their parents and caregivers at the US-Mexico border. More recently, he’s pushed the administration to accelerate the deportation of undocumented children.

Miller, 41, who is himself the descendant of Jewish immigrants to the US and grew up in liberal Santa Monica, California, came to reject his home town, viewing California as a failed state that had been perverted by mass immigration. Eventually, he came to see immigration as a leftwing plot to undermine his vision of a traditional United States.

In more than a decade by Trump’s side, Miller has worked with the president to wrest extreme executive authority, to undermine Congress and the judiciary and defy oversight – in large part to advance his anti-immigrant campaign.
“He never backs down,” said Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth in a congratulatory social media post, calling Miller a true patriot.

Democratic lawmakers who’ve re-taken control of Congress, governor’s offices and statehouses may have to spend much of the next two years bringing Miller’s ambitions to heel. Human rights activists and advocates on behalf of immigrants are immediately calling on congressmembers to do everything they can to stop Miller.

US representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is poised to lead the House oversight committee next year, warned that Miller “should lawyer up” – promising to investigate him and his involvement in the administration’s mass deportation scheme.

Senator Alex Padilla said that if Trump was doubling down, “so will we”, promising to use “every tool at our disposal – oversight, investigations, subpoenas, and our leverage over federal funding – to expose this administration’s abuse of power and hold those responsible accountable”.

But even with full control of Congress, Democrats will likely have a limited ability to rein in the administration’s immigration enforcement agencies – which are bloated with $70bn in funding through 2029. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is poised to massively expand its workforce. Immigration arrests and detentions are already at an all-time high.

Miller, meanwhile, has shown a unique unwillingness to concede – in 2018, he reportedly sank a deal that would have gotten Trump $25bn funding for a border wall in exchange for a provision that would have provided permanent protection for undocumented immigrants who had come to the US as children.

It hasn’t seemed to faze him that the administration’s policies have alienated the coalition of voters who elected Trump into office in 2024 – including a large contingency of Latino voters. And he is unlikely to be moved by voters’ backlash against the Trump administration’s most extreme policies.
“This puts him in a position of greater power to wreak havoc,” Al-Juburi said.

articles.title: Ben Roberts-Smith collaborates with gym business run by influencer that sold ‘war crimes’ pre-workout supplement
articles.summary:
Zero Limits supplements is co-owned by right-wing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as ‘Big Chocky’

Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company…

blocks.text: Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a right-wing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”.

Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing t-shirts and gym wear.

In October, he also appeared in a social media video collaboration between his brand and Zero Limits supplements, co-owned by right-wing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as “Big Chocky”.

Roberts-Smith, Katelaris and others were filmed during a gym workout, with on-screen graphics reading “Zero Limits Supplements x Epic 1 Two”. Both brands were labelled “collaborators” on the video, which is also published on the Instagram grids of both brands.

Months earlier, Zero Limits had repeatedly posted online about a product titled “war crimes”, an energy supplement in the flavour “kill or capture cola”. Its label depicted a hooded captive on a chair in a room with an Australian flag on the wall, and a tall figure wearing a balaclava and military-style clothing.
In a video on 26 July, Katelaris promoted the product while holding a tub at the gym.
“You wanna drink out of a prosthetic leg? You wanna re-enact a Sparta kick? You wanna execute your workout?” he said.
“War crimes, it’s the pre-workout for you.”

Zero Limits, which says it is “veteran owned and operated”, does not currently list the “war crimes” product on its website, and Roberts-Smith is not shown endorsing, referencing or using that particular product.

The former soldier has praised another product from Zero Limits, posting an Instagram story – since shared by the brand – from Epic 1 Two’s Instagram page of himself drinking a separate pre-workout drink.

Roberts-Smith gave the brand a “massive shout out” and told followers to “get on their website and take a look”, sharing a link to its website. Roberts-Smith also last week appeared on the Zero Limits podcast, hosted by another founder of the supplements company of the same name.
Roberts-Smith was in April arrested and charged with five counts of war crime – murder, in relation to three incidents stemming from his service in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has denied the charges, saying in a statement after his arrest: “As I’ve always maintained: I categorically deny all of these allegations … I will be taking this opportunity to finally clear my name. I’m proud of my service in Afghanistan.”

The three incidents allegedly involved Afghan nationals being shot dead by Roberts-Smith, or a subordinate under his command, while he was present, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in April.

Roberts-Smith was previously found in a defamation suit – using the civil standard of the balance of probabilities – to have murdered unarmed civilians while serving in the Australian Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) in Afghanistan.

The federal court found to the lower civil standard that Roberts-Smith kicked Afghan man Ali Jan in the chest, sending him falling backwards over a cliff before he landed on the ground. The court found that Roberts-Smith then ordered another soldier to shoot him dead.
Roberts-Smith was also accused in media reporting of shooting an unarmed prisoner who had a prosthetic leg. The leg was later used as a drinking vessel by soldiers.
Zero Limits, Katelaris and Roberts-Smith were contacted for comment.
In a statement via a lawyer, Zero Limits did not respond to specific questions, only answering: “The products are great, make sure you check them out.”
In a statement via the same lawyer, Katelaris also did not respond to specific questions, but said: “If you thought this was wild, wait until next week’s campaign drops.”

Katelaris lists himself as a “co-owner” of the supplements brand in his Instagram bio. He also promotes a range of merchandise under his own name in support of Roberts-Smith, including “I stand with BRS” t-shirts, hats, hoodies and stubby coolers.

articles.title: Man in custody after being found in vehicle near White House with guns
articles.summary:
Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos arrested by secret service after telling officers voices told him to kill Donald Trump

The US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and…

blocks.text: The US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill Donald Trump.

The arrest Thursday night happened after secret service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. US officials said the suspect – Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican president.

Shortly after, officers discovered the suspect’s vehicle had been reported stolen and he had three firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition. This is the latest in a series of arrests the secret service and other law enforcement agencies have made against individuals who have threatened Trump or his family members’ lives since he returned to office last year.

The statement described Chrinos as an immigrant from Venezuela who is in the country illegally after entering the US through Texas in March 2024. DHS said he had been charged and was in US Marshals Service custody.
The White House did not provide comment, instead referring to DHS and the US secret service.

articles.title: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest
articles.summary: Ousted Paraguayan president Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied…

image.caption: Former paraguayan president Santiago Peña — seen here addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September — was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust. (Caitlin Ochs/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Ousted Paraguayan president Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.
Arrest ordered shortly after Senate removed him as president

In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies. The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, cutting nearly three million customers off from their savings and bank cards and setting off a political crisis.

Prosecutors ordered that Peña be held at his home until he can be brought before their economic crimes and anti-corruption unit, according to a letter to the national police commander. The attorney general's office confirmed to The Associated Press that he had been detained there. The order also called for the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, the former central bank chief Peña appointed. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo was in custody.

Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing.

Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. He inherits a government under pressure to return depositors' money and punish those behind Ueno's collapse.

A veteran of the long-ruling conservative Colorado party, Alliana, 52, is a former governor of the southern province of Ñeembucú and a former speaker of the lower house. He has not escaped the scandal entirely: Prosecutors are also investigating him, and on Thursday lawmakers shelved an opposition bid to impeach him.

Peña's removal also bars him from the lifetime Senate seat granted to elected former presidents under Paraguay's Constitution, denying him the parliamentary immunity that would accompany it. Prosecutors are also investigating current and former central bank and pension fund officials.
People protest against the government and Ueno Bank in Asunción, Paraguay, on Wednesday. (Jorge Saenz/The Associated Press)

Peña had submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it. His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that lawmakers should have approved his departure instead of pressing ahead with the impeachment trial.
In a farewell message released shortly before the verdict, Peña expressed hope his departure would spare Paraguay further harm.
"I do not want my presence to be a cause of greater division or instability," he wrote. "My responsibility is to put the country above my personal fate."
Growing public outrage

Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno's failure marched through downtown Asunción chanting, "Santi Peña to Tacumbú!" — a reference to the capital's main prison.
"This was an enormous betrayal of trust," said Yinal López, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno.

Ueno's implosion has plunged Paraguay into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade — and at dizzying speed. Regulators seized the bank before dawn Tuesday. By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado Party turned on him, led by former president Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña's longtime mentor. By Friday, his interior minister, chief of staff, legal adviser and political adviser had all quit.

It was a staggering reversal of fortunes for Peña, a telegenic technocrat and a former International Monetary Fund economist who owed his rapid political ascent to Cartes. The tobacco magnate, among Paraguay's richest men, made Peña his finance minister and twice backed him for president over rival factions' objections.
'Like a Shakespearean drama'

Once in office, though, Peña quietly amassed a rival power base, analysts say. Ueno Bank, flush with public deposits, became the centrepiece of both his business empire and his effort to win over provincial governors as he sought to escape Cartes' shadow.
"It's like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron," said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research centre. "But he did so on very fragile grounds."
Police stand guard outside of a closed Ueno Bank branch in Nemby, Paraguay, on Tuesday. (Cesar Olmedo/Reuters)

Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him demanded answers from the central bank about Ueno's lending, citing leaked internal reports that warned its loans to related companies put its solvency at risk. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña's leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protégé.
"Cartes put the nail in the coffin," said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. "Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry."
A view of the headquarters of Ueno Bank in Asunción, on Tuesday. (Jorge Saenz/The Associated Press)

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp: Prosecution had its chance but failed; VP begins defense Monday
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday hit back at the prosecution, saying the latter had its chance, but failed. It also said Duterte will begin her defense on Monday, November 9.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 8:02am
The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday hit back at the prosecution, saying the latter had its chance, but failed. It also said Duterte will begin her defense on Monday, November 9.
"The prosecution had its chance. It failed. On Monday, the Vice President begins her defense," Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for Duterte, said in a statement.

"We apparently live in two worlds. One where due process and fairness still reign—where an accused is not condemned before she is heard, and where allegations must be proven with clear and convincing evidence presented in court. The other is wherever Atty. Lorna Kapunan and her colleagues have decided these rules no longer apply," he added.

"One world seeks the truth. The other desperately tries to persuade an increasingly skeptical public with asinine sound bites built on half-truths and malicious speculation, spewed out in daily, obtrusive, and nauseating press briefings and interviews," Panelo said.
Duterte's spokesperson made the comments a day after private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said Duterte is the best evidence against herself.

Kapunan made the response when asked if the vice president taking the witness stand will enable her to answer the impeachable allegations, mainly amassing around P817 million worth of unexplained wealth.

“If the Vice President appears before the impeachment court, she will be the best evidence against herself due to her demeanor, the way she answers. Remember, when she was summoned in House [hearings], she refused to take an oath. Would she even take an oath to tell the truth and nothing but the truth?” Kapunan said.

“The only one she can blame is herself. She gave evidence against herself by declaring in her SALN interest in these companies,” Kapunan said, referring to declared assets of the vice president such as Metro City Chow Foods Corp. and GenCorp. Foods Industries Inc. which Duterte has not divested from even amid a constitutional prohibition.

Kapunan noted that the vice president’s statements of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALNs)—the same documents in which she did not declare cash on hand or in bank from 2019 to 2025, despite bank officials testifying that she had bank deposits—were signed by Duterte under oath.
"That is the situation of the VP. She is giving evidence against herself," she said.

Kapunan also said the P776 million in remittances sent to Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared banana chips company and an asset listed in the vice president’s husband's SALN, was another clear-cut indication of unexplained wealth, as the amount was not reflected in the Duterte couple’s joint SALN.
The defense team of Duterte has listed at least 24 initial witnesses it intends to present upon the resumption of the impeachment trial next week.
The impeachment trial of the vice president will resume on Monday, November 9, at 10 a.m. —KG, GMA News
