articles.title: U.S. sanctions Canadian money-exchange businesses connected to Iranian regime, Ryan Wedding
articles.summary: The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head…

image.caption: 'Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,' Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement. (Nathan Howard/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada·New

The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
Companies in Canada gave sanctioned Iranian entities 'financial lifeline,' treasury says

The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.

"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.

items: Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada

blocks.text: The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.

In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada.
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:

items: Diverse ‌Trade ⁠Inc., doing business as Million Exchange in Ontario.
1380079 BC Limited, doing business as Amin Exchange in B.C.
Top PC Technician Inc., operating in Ontario.
NIA Nations Currency Ltd., based in B.C.
2397639 Ontario Ltd., doing business as Farah Exchange.
CCC Inc. in Ontario.
B Galaxy Inc., doing business as Cryptoyal from the same Ontario location as CCC Inc.
Darvish Exchange in Ontario.

blocks.text: The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.

In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.

items: Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran

blocks.text: In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January.
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.
Ryan Wedding’s path from Olympian to wanted fugitive
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations
articles.summary: Friday's resolution by academic staff is largely symbolic as they do not have the power to remove those in charge of the university.

blocks.text: Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.
The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.
All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.
Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.

The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".
It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.
It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.
The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, responded to the vote's outcome in a statement, saying: "We recently learned that Cornell's Faculty Senate made a finding of no confidence in the Central Administration's ability to address the longstanding crisis of sexual assault at Cornell.
"We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information."
Giuffra added: "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

The board of trustees, which does have the power to fire Kotlikoff, said in a statement that it "remains confident" that he and his administration "are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus".

Trustees board chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling, added: "This confidence is rooted not only in the administration's actions to date and plans moving forward, but also in its track record of navigating complex problems."
She also said that the vote of no confidence "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable".

Backlash against Cornell has been intense since Doe filed her lawsuit in September. She reported the alleged assault to campus police after it happened but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time.

Cornell, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, has acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case and has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review of the case. It also recently announced a series of measures due assault, including cancelling fraternity parties.
New York state prosecutors, led by Attorney General Letitia James, are carrying out their own investigation to decide if criminal charges are warranted.
Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that state police would investigate any future sexual offence complaints at the university.

articles.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
articles.summary: The US president's promotion of Miller, a loyal partisan firebrand to be his new chief of staff sets up likely clashes with Congress.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
By
North America correspondent
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.

He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.

Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.

The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?
Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.

Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.

blocks.caption: Stephen Miller and Donald Trump appear in the Oval Office in front of an American flag and a statue of George Washington

blocks.text: On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.

Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.

"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.

At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Paraguay: President Santiago Pena under house arrest over bank crisis
articles.summary: Paraguay’s Senate has ousted President Santiago Pena over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government. Millions of customers' accounts are frozen, with public pension and health care funds…

image.caption: Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties (FILE: 03/03/2025)Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's Senate on Friday impeached President Santiago Pena over a banking crisis that left millions of people unable to access their deposits.
Senators voted overwhelmingly to remove Pena for misconduct in office.
The move cleared the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to succeed him. He will serve the rest of the presidential term, which ends in August 2028.

Pena had already resigned on Thursday, but by impeaching and convicting him instead of accepting his resignation, senators stripped him of the lifetime Senate seat and immunity granted to former presidents, leaving him vulnerable to prosecution.
Following the Senate vote, prosecutors ordered the arrest of the ousted president alongside former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo as part of a criminal investigation.
Officials later said Pena was placed under house arrest pending a decision by the public prosecutor's office on the final charges against him.
Dozens of ​protesters gathered outside ​his residence ‌in the capital Asuncion, while police maintained ​a ⁠security cordon around the property.
Why did Pena face impeachment?
Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties.
The bank's accounts — also used to process pension payments — are frozen, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money. Ueno also held hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds.
Pena's resignation on Thursday followed the withdrawal of support by Congress President Basilio Nunez and ruling conservative Colorado Party leader Horacio Cartes.

Thirty-five opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents had submitted impeachment articles in the 80-seat Chamber of Deputies, accusing Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to Ueno.
Pena sold his shares in Ueno Holding, whose businesses include the bank, in April 2025. Lawmakers also cited two loans he received from Ueno as part of allegations of improper financial gain.

They alleged improper presidential interference in the Social Security Institute, known as IPS, and preferential treatment for Ueno. IPS manages pension and health care funds for most Paraguayan workers and held $355 million at the bank — about 9% of its investments, according to financial manager Gladys Vera.

The motion also questioned Pena's 2023 appointment of central bank chief Carvallo, who previously chaired Financiera Ueno. According to the document, the central bank approved the company's conversion into a bank just 83 days after his appointment.
What happened to Ueno Bank?
Ueno served about 2.94 million customers, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

As of last month, the bank said it held roughly $800 million in public-sector deposits — about a quarter of its total deposits — including money from the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

blocks.caption: People took the the streets of Asuncion on WednesdayImage: Jorge Saenz/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's central bank ordered a resolution or closure process Tuesday after finding that Ueno's solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum.
Ueno's app, card payments and transfers stopped working, while branches closed, leaving customers queuing outside unable to withdraw their savings.
Hundreds of employees of Ueno and other companies in its parent conglomerate protested outside the Labor Ministry Thursday, demanding unpaid wages and severance.
Retirees, depositors, students and workers had marched through Asuncion a day earlier, demanding Pena's impeachment and holding signs saying "Give us back our money."
What have authorities done?

Authorities detained eight senior executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud.
Lawyers for several detainees said they needed time to review the allegations before commenting.
Pena had sought to reassure customers in a video message Wednesday, pledging legislation "that will return to every saver what they are entitled to as quickly as possible."
The crisis also forced him to cancel his attendance at the Ibero-American summit in Madrid.
Pena, a conservative economist, took office in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Editor's Note: This piece, originally published on November 5, was updated on November 7 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
articles.summary:
Primary school students bested 200,000 competitors across New South Wales to reach the Premier’s Spelling Bee finals in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales. The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition. Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

blocks.caption: The tension is palpable on stage at the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.
To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.
The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.
Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.
In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.
“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.

blocks.caption: Alesha Kahfandi missed ‘antepenultimate’ but is tied for runner-up. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: But the show must go on.
after newsletter promotion

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.
“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.
But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”
“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

blocks.caption: Maximilian Lumley wins second place in the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee in Penrith in Sydney’s west. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”
Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.
“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”
Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.
“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

articles.title: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay at start of South America tour
articles.summary: Pope Leo has arrived in Uruguay at the start of a 12-day trip through three South American nations. His trip, which is intense with a packed itinerary, comes just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.

image.caption: Uruguay's President Yamandu Orsi welcomed Pope Leo as he landed in Carrasco International Airport Image: Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay on Friday at the start of a grueling 12-day tour through three South American countries, just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff told reporters he was very happy to be in Uruguay, having flown a nearly 14-hour flight from Rome to get to Montevideo.
"I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward," he told reporters aboard the papal plane.
Leo hit the ground running on arrival, drawing huge crowds in Montevideo as he pulled into town in his open-sided popemobile.
The Vatican estimated 30,000 people had turned out to watch him go by and attend his first event in a country that is largely secular and where membership in the Church is declining.

"In an age ‌when ​differences can easily become a source of conflict, persevering ​in respect for the law, negotiation and the ⁠patient ​search for ​agreements is a service ​that Uruguay ‌can continue to offer its neighbors," ​Leo ⁠told crowds in Montevideo's main square.
Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance, was present there too.
Leo is then planning to visit the Casavalle neighborhood, which is notorious for its high rates of poverty and violence.
With starting in Uruguay, Leo marks the first papal visit to the country in nearly four decades, with Pope John Paul II having last visited in 1988.
What to know about Pope Leo's taxing itinerary
The pontiff will spend three days in Uruguay before heading on to Argentina on Sunday.
He then travels to Peru, where he spent half his priestly life, before he was elected pontiff last year. He became a naturalized Peruvian citizen in 2015.
Latin America is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, for whom the pope is their spiritual leader. However, fewer and fewer people on the continent identify as Catholic.
Enthusiasm around Leo's visit a surprise in Uruguay

Uruguay, the most secular Latin American country, was the first country in the world to legalize recreational marijuana use and has since legalized abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all against opposition from the Catholic Church.
However, the enthusiasm around Leo's visit has come as a bit of a surprise, with tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium selling out in just two days.

blocks.caption: The pope is expected to express opposition to some of the more liberal policies enacted in UruguayImage: Lucas Aguayo Araos/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: What will Pope Leo do in Argentina?
On Sunday, Leo will cross over to neighboring Argentina, the home of his papal predecessor Francis, who, however, disappointed his native compatriots by never returning home as pope.
At the beginning of Francis's papacy, some 71% of Argentinians identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2024, this had fallen to 58%.

blocks.caption: Leo will hope his visit makes up for the refusal by his predecessor to visit his home countryImage: Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo is set to meet with Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has come under criticism from the Catholic Church for his sweeping cuts that have hampered programs for the poor and needy.
He is also planning to meet with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives.
Pope Leo to return to Peru for last leg of trip
The final leg of the trip, on Wednesday, will see Leo return to Peru, where he lived and preached for two decades.
There is excitement about his visit to Peru, with the pope planning to celebrate Mass in his old diocese of Chiclayo as well as in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
The pope will also celebrate Mass in the former Incan capital city of Cusco before honoring Peru's indigenous population by traveling to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon.
The excitement can be seen in the street vendors selling T-shirts and rosaries with his likeness, while bakeries have been selling Leo bread.
Peru has also seen a weakening of the faithful in recent years, with the Catholic population falling from 76% in 2013-2014 to around 67% now.

blocks.caption: Peruvian Catholics have shown particular interest in the pope's visit as a type of homecomingImage: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: In B.C.'s Great Bear Rainforest, DNA testing crucial to finding grizzly behind deadly attack
articles.summary: The investigation into a suspected fatal grizzly attack this week includes DNA profiling to identify the animal responsible.

image.caption: The B.C. Conservation Officer Service said it had captured one bear, and work is underway to determine if it is behind the deaths of two women near Bella Coola, B.C. (Amir Said/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Updated
The investigation into a suspected fatal grizzly attack this week includes DNA profiling to identify the animal responsible.
Forensics expert says finding a killer bear is very similar to using DNA from crime scenes to find suspects
On Friday, the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said it had captured one bear, and work is underway to determine if it is behind the killings.

Techniques used will include cross-referencing DNA samples from the captured bear against a DNA profile created using materials left at the scene where a mother and daughter were found dead on a trail just outside of Bella Coola on B.C.'s Central Coast.

Forensics expert Dean Hildebrand — founder of the B.C. Institute of Technology Forensics DNA Lab, which is not involved in the investigation — said the use of DNA for an investigation is "very similar to what we do in humans."

items: Mother and daughter killed in suspected grizzly attack were 'two peas in a pod,' family says
More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: Hildebrand said only trace amounts of DNA would be needed to create the profile, which can then be held indefinitely as an electronic file to check against any future attacks.

"We have a crime scene index in Canada where we get DNA profiles from crime scenes unsolved. They go into a database and they just sit there and those things can link crime scenes together until the other side comes together where you get the offender. So it would be exactly analogous to this."
LISTEN | How DNA is used to track grizzlies after an attack:
Daybreak North5:34Using DNA to find a deadly grizzly bear
DNA profile also created in 2025 attack
B.C. Conservation Officer Service Insp. Jeff Tyre said if they catch the bear responsible for the attack, it will be killed.

He also said they would also check the sample from this week's attack against the DNA profile created for the grizzly behind a November 2025 incident where a group of students and teachers were injured by a bear in Bella Coola.
Though eight bears were trapped and released in the aftermath of that case, the bear was never found.

The search continues for a grizzly bear believed responsible for a deadly attack on a mother and daughter near Bella Coola, B.C., this week. Members of the public are urged to avoid the Snooka West Trail area. (B.C. Conservation Officer Service)
But he also said DNA testing is a crucial element of the investigation because there are "so many bears" in the area, making it difficult to count.
Bella Coola, about 400 kilometres northwest of Vancouver as the crow flies, is part of the Great Bear Rainforest, a region protected in part because of its importance to grizzly bears.
Coastal First Nations, including the Nuxalk Nation whose territory encompasses Bella Coola, have long coexisted with the animals that are a crucial part of their culture.

items: Suggested curfew, night patrols in place following suspected fatal grizzly attack near Bella Coola
Call to renew licensed grizzly bear hunting met with pushback from B.C. conservationists

blocks.text: "Nuxalk have lived with bears for thousands of years, and we consider them to be our kin," Elected Chief Samuel Schooner said in an emailed statement this week. Schooner said his community is taking time to heal from this week's attack, which has reopened trauma from last year, but emphasized that any decisions about how to live with bears moving forward will come from within.

In the meantime, Nuxalk leadership is working with conservation officers and RCMP to provide support and protection, which includes providing escorts for children going to school and offering rides to anyone who needs to get around.
With files from Daybreak North

articles.title: 4 reasons to watch Canada in the women's hockey world championship
articles.summary: Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship

image.caption: Canada's players celebrate their first goal goal score by Jessie Eldridge (9) during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship
Canada has shaken up the team at every level after some heartbreaking losses

Yes, there's the patriotism of cheering for your country, and yes, there's the Canada/U.S. rivalry, but those aren't the only reasons to watch Team Canada in the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship.
Canada dominated Sweden 5-1 in its world women's hockey championship opener Friday to kick off the 11-day, 10-nation tournament in Denmark. Their next game is Sunday, when they face Japan.
The U.S. and Canada are the tournament favourites, continuing a long-standing cross-border rivalry. Canada has won 13 world titles followed by the U.S. with 11 spanning the previous 24 championships.
But this year, there are even more reasons it's worth paying attention to the Canadian team. Here are a few of them:
Jesse Eldridge leads Canada past Sweden at the worlds
1. The youngest lineup in decades
To quote Hockey Canada's Women's Worlds preview, "the kids have arrived."

The average age of this roster is 26 years, two months and 22 days — the youngest roster Canada has played at the Women’s Worlds since 2013, Hockey Canada notes. Three of the youngest players are debuting in Denmark: Rosalie Tremblay (age 18), Hayley McDonald (age 18), and Sara Manness (age 19).

items: 7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: Three other collegiate players, 19-year-old Chloe Primerano (University of Minnesota), 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer (University of Minnesota Duluth) and 23-year-old Ève Gascon (University of Minnesota Duluth) return for their second world championship.
The oldest player is goaltender Ann-Renée Desbien, who is 32.

Canada's goalkeeper Ann-Renée Desbien makes a save during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark on Friday. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)
2. Poulin is out
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin has been sidelined due to knee surgery after tearing her ACL last spring, leaving the Canadian team without its captain for the first time in more than a decade.

Poulin is widely regarded as one of the greatest women's hockey players of all time. She's won three Olympic gold medals, scoring the winning goal in all three of those gold-medal games to earn the nickname "Captain Clutch."

items: What to know for the women's hockey world championship
7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: A five-time Olympian, Poulin is also the all-time leading goal scorer for the Canadian women's team at the Winter Games with 20. With her out, Canada is playing in its first international tournament without Poulin on the roster since she made her national team debut in 2009.
Defender Renata Fast and forward Laura Stacey are sharing Canada's captaincy in Denmark.
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin provides update about her health
3. New head coach and management
The Canadians ended last season with a heartbreaking loss in the Olympic gold-medal game against the Americans. Since then, there's been change at all levels for Canada.

The group has new leadership, starting with Hockey Hall of Famer Danièle Sauvageau, who returns to the Hockey Canada fold as GM of the senior national team. Ottawa Charge GM Mike Hirshfeld and PWHL Detroit GM Manon Rhéaume are serving as assistant GMs.

items: Mix of young, veteran players invited to Canadian women's hockey team camp

blocks.text: There's also a new head coach: Kori Cheverie, who led Sauvageau's Victoire to a Walter Cup in the spring. Cheverie has been an assistant with the national team since before the 2022 Olympic gold-medal win.

Montreal Victoire head coach Kori Cheverie hoists the Walter Cup alongside general manager Daniele Sauvageau during the Montreal Victoire's victory celebration in Montreal in May. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
4. Coming off some big losses

The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 worlds and claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and the Olympic gold medal at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.
Canada was also swept in the Canada/U.S. Rivalry Series that concluded last December. So now, with a fresh roster and without its greatest star, Canada is looking to reclaim the championship.

The final is set for Nov. 16. While it's not necessarily guaranteed that Team Canada will make it, it's been Canada vs. the U.S. in 23 out of the last 24 finals. The lone exception came in 2019, when host Finland shocked the Canadians in the semis before losing a controversial final against the States.
With files from CBC's Karissa Donkin and Jesse Campigotto, Reuters and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Canada's foreign minister urges G7 to turn up heat on Putin after deadly Ukraine strike
articles.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is pressing G7 allies to intensify pressure on Russia after an attack on a Ukrainian aid distribution site killed 53 people. Anand says the international…

image.caption: A rescuer uses a drone detector during a search operation at the site of an underground shelter that was used as a humanitarian aid hub in Russia's Zaporizhzhia region. The hub was hit by a Russian airstrike on Monday. (Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is pressing G7 allies to intensify pressure on Russia after an attack on a Ukrainian aid distribution site killed 53 people. Anand says the international community must strengthen sanctions and military support, and confront Moscow directly when world leaders gather for December's G20 summit in Florida.
Anand demands stronger collective action as Russian attacks intensify

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says she'll make a point of pushing her G7 colleagues to take further, concerted action against Russia following this week's horrific strike on an aid distribution site in Ukraine.

Anand will be meeting with her counterparts this weekend in Paris and said Friday that the issue of Moscow's unrelenting campaign targeting civilians should also be a topic of conversation at the G20 later this year near Miami.

The death toll from Russia's bombing earlier this week of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region rose on Friday to 53, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure caused renewed power outages in seven Ukrainian regions, the country's deputy energy minister said.

items: Ukraine's winter warning to Canada: Help us keep the lights on

blocks.text: Anand said the strikes, which came as U.S. First Lady Melania Trump tried to further mediation efforts, "necessitates collective action over and above what we are putting on the table" in terms of sanctions and economic and military support.
"I will be raising the need for collective effort with my G7 counterparts," Anand said following a meeting in Ottawa with her Austrian counterpart.

U.S. President Donald Trump has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the mid-December gathering of G20 world leaders at his Doral, Fla., golf club. Putin has not yet decided whether he will accept the invitation.
Anand said the world community shouldn't waste the opportunity to confront Russia.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with Austrian Foreign Affairs Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger on Friday in Ottawa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

"At the G20 in December, this issue must be raised amongst countries at the table, especially given that Russia will be represented there and it will be an opportunity to speak directly to them," Anand said.
At a recent meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, in preparation for the upcoming summit, Anand confronted Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

She said she sat directly across the table from Lavrov, looked him straight in the eye and condemned Russia's "horrific crimes" and full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Anand and some European ministers refused to participate in the routine "family photo" because she didn't want to be pictured alongside Lavrov.

items: Death toll from Russian attack in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region climbs to 53

blocks.text: Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said she is particularly worried about the recent strikes in Zaporizhzhia because the region hosts Ukraine's largest nuclear power complex, which has been under Russia occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion.
She said she's in favour of further tightening international pressure on the Kremlin.
"There's one person only to decide to stop the war and it would stop immediately. This is Vladimir Putin," Meinl-Reisinger said.
"He is not able to win this war militarily. So we have to continue to put pressure that he is ready to negotiate for real this time."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
