articles.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.summary: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.

blocks.text: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.

Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.

The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

articles.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
articles.summary: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and…

image.caption: Travellers are seen at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague on Friday after Czech police registered bomb threats against flights arriving and departing from the airport, amid a series of similar threats affecting flights across Europe. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

blocks.text: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations to conduct security sweeps.

No explosives have been found, and the threats have so far proved unfounded. But the spate of hoaxes that affected a number of flights, airports and, as of Friday, news broadcasters has raised concern over the widening impact if the threats continue to spread.

It's not yet clear if the incidents are linked, but the bomb threat hoaxes come on the heels of other European disruptions, including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
Here is what we know about the hoaxes targeting airlines and broadcasters in Europe.
When did the threats begin?
What appeared to be a co-ordinated wave of bomb threats targeting European air traffic began on Tuesday.

At least seven flights and a cruise ship received hoax bomb threats, triggering emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and temporary airport closures in countries including Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain.
A second wave was reported on Thursday, with at least 27 flights affected.
Bomb threats force multiple flights in Europe to make emergency landings

On Friday, Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain.
How are newsrooms involved?

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov" claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.
The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

Garda members work outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE on Friday after staff were evacuated from the site following a bomb threat. The broadcaster has claimed the bomb threat is from the same group that has been behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)
How are the threats sent?

Bomb threats against planes are often communicated to airlines, airports or authorities through anonymous emails or phone calls claiming that an explosive device is on board. Authorities do not always disclose how threats are delivered, because doing so could encourage copycats and compromise investigations.

A Prague airport representative told CNN on Thursday that they had received a threat from an anonymous email addressed to the airport, and Czech police said similar emails went to other European airports.

Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, told Reuters that an airline's security department first runs the report through a checklist. It then alerts the authorities, who may scramble fighter jets or divert the plane to a designated airport for a full sweep.
What are the risks?
The vast majority of bomb threats turn out to be false alarms, though all must be treated as real until investigated, which means authorities are forced to scramble to rule out any danger.
No explosive device has been found on the planes affected this week, but every airline must decide whether a threat is credible and act accordingly.
A spokesperson for the British government called this week's incidents "malicious hoax threats" and said it has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world."

items: String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe
Bomb threats affect at least 27 flights, leading to emergency landings at several European airports

blocks.text: Airlines are not new to bomb threats, but aviation security experts say the apparent co-ordination and timing of the current incidents is unusual.
All planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.
Who is behind the threats?
Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government.

The incidents come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response.
Countries affected by the disruptions, including Denmark, Poland and ​Romania, have previously accused Moscow. Russia denies any involvement.
An EasyJet aircraft takes off at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State," a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia.
Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.
What is their goal?

Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said bomb threats can stem from a wide range of motives, including political grievances, activist campaigns, criminal activity, online groups or state-linked hybrid operations.

European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen says that since 2022, Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference.
“We are under attack all the time,” she told Reuters. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilize our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.”
“It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations. Quite often, it is Russia.”
How have airlines been affected?
Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority.

Even a false alarm can disrupt airlines' operations, with plane diversions and thorough security inspections causing delays for passengers. Carriers typically bear additional costs including fuel, passenger rebooking, crew disruption and aircraft diversions.
Schouten said a sweep means unloading passengers and baggage, searching the aircraft and reloading. That can push crews past duty limits and lead to missed connections and cancellations.
People gather outside the offices of Irish national broadcaster RTE as officials conduct a security sweep after a reported bomb threat on Friday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)
Air France-KLM chief executive Ben Smith said on Thursday he had never previously seen threats reported in such a co-ordinated fashion.

"We're quite confident that we have in place what we need to ensure that it has minimal or no impact on our operation," Smith told reporters. "So we have no ask today of our governments to change the way they manage these types of situations."
Which airlines, airports have been affected?

blocks.text: What measures are being taken?
Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice-president of the European Cockpit Association.
Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

articles.title: Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck
articles.summary: Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive…

image.caption: A Cybertruck might be parked at sites like Tesla's Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg, but the vast pickup is not road legal in Germany [FILE: April 23, 2026]Image: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

blocks.caption: Cybertrucks fit on LA's wide roads with relative ease, but that's not the case everywhereImage: Barry King/Alamy/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did the Cybertruck fail to attract customers?
Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."
For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."
However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.
Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.
Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.
Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

blocks.caption: The agressive set-square design appealed to some of the more eccentric and well-financed police departments in the US like casino capital Las VegasImage: Ty ONeil/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How far short of Musk's sales targets did the Cybertruck fall?
Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.
But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.
At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.
For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

blocks.caption: SpaceX purchased a vast fleet of Cybertrucks in 2025, perhaps feeling the futuristic styling fits the company's aesthetics, or perhaps as a favor to a friendImage: Charles Briggs/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the story with the next pet project, the Cybercab?
The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.
Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

blocks.caption: Tesla held a Cybercab launch party in Ausitin in September this yearImage: Bob Daemmrich/ZUMA/picture alliance

articles.title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
articles.summary: Jim Messina tells the BBC that after Democrats' midterm victories he's talked to "over two dozen campaigns", with some already hiring staff.

blocks.text: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.
"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.
He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.
He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"
Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.
"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.
"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."

Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".
"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.

items: PODCAST: Hear more from Jim Messina on Americast

blocks.text: Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.

"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.
Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".
The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

articles.title: Data center protesters break into Microsoft site in Amsterdam
articles.summary: Protesters are demanding a pause in data center construction in Europe. Campaigners planning protests in 16 countries say the AI building boom threatens water supplies, power grids and climate goals.

image.caption: The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operatingImage: Koen van Weel/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, climbing cranes and hanging balloons while police stood by.

The action opened two days of planned protests in 16 countries, with campaigners demanding a pause in major artificial intelligence data center construction over concerns about electricity, water and environmental damage.
What happened in Amsterdam?
More than 100 activists gathered at the site, marching arm in arm before entering. Some danced or carried placards reading: "Screw your data center."
"These data centers are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said.

blocks.caption: Image: Koen van Weel/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than $1 billion (€890 million) in the project, urged protesters to leave safely and discuss their concerns.
Microsoft said it respected people's right to express their views peacefully but did not condone unlawful actions.

The Stop Dirty Data Centres coalition said other planned actions included a march in Dublin, a protest outside Poland's parliament and a demonstration against another Microsoft data center in Denmark.
Why are campaigners opposing data centers?
The protest group said more demonstrations are planned in several European countries on Saturday, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the UK.
Campaigners say the facilities strain electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for resources and threaten climate goals.
They also raise concerns about job losses and the concentration of power in technology companies.
The coalition said it was not calling for existing data centers to close. It wants governments to establish clearer rules before further large-scale construction proceeds.
Technology companies argue that data centers provide essential infrastructure for AI and cloud services used by businesses, governments and consumers.

The dispute comes amid growing scrutiny of the industry's expansion. A Google project in Finland faces a criminal investigation over land clearances, while Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental rules for data centers.
The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operating.

articles.title: Despite Russia impasse, Germany still hoping to host Men's Ice Hockey World Championship
articles.summary: A week after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey, the way forward remains unclear. Berlin is seeking a solution that will allow Germany to host next year's…

image.caption: Skoda has long been the main sponsor of the Men's World Ice Hockey ChampionshipImage: Vit Simanek/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A German government spokesman has said that despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since last Friday's decision, several leading ice hockey nations, including Finland, Sweden and Czechia have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada late next month, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russian participation would render the hosting of the World Championship "practically impossible, both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

However, he also said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the World Championship – as planned – in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf next May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled. However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore—through dialogue—how we can still ensure the tournament takes place," he said.

Following last Friday's CAS decision ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as World Championship host.
German visa restrictions on Russians in place

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a German interior ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult due to restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy'—and we will certainly not pretend that there is," Martin Giese said.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."
Consensus remains elusive
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision – before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark – and with the clock ticking towards the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26,

articles.title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance
ByBernd Debusmann
White House reporter
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways.
The 2026 winners who now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

items: Dozens eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

blocks.text: Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is an oil spill and how does it affect communities?
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported an oil spill in Mariveles, Bataan, on Friday, affecting approximately 500 square meters of coastal waters.

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 12:05am
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported an oil spill in Mariveles, Bataan, on Friday, affecting approximately 500 square meters of coastal waters.

In the Philippines, damage caused by oil spills reached P4.93 billion in 2023, accounting for 53% of the total damage from human-induced disasters recorded that year, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
What are oil spills and how does it affect us?

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) defines crude oil as a fossil fuel used to manufacture a wide array of petroleum products, ranging from transportation fuels like gasoline to materials such as asphalt, plastics, soaps, and paints.
NOAA noted that oil spills can occur on both small and large scales, with either posing significant threats to marine life.

“Most of these spills are small, for example, when oil spills while refueling a ship. But these spills can still cause damage, especially if they happen in sensitive environments, like beaches, mangroves, and wetlands,” the agency explained.
“Large oil spills are major, dangerous disasters. These tend to happen when pipelines break, big oil tanker ships sink, or drilling operations go wrong,” it added.

One of the Philippines' notable large-scale oil spills occurred in 2024, when the MT Terranova sank off the coast of Bataan while carrying 1.4 million liters of industrial fuel oil. During cleanup operations, the PCG reported recovering more than 1 million liters of oily waste.
Impacts
Oil spills threaten marine life as well as the livelihoods and safety of coastal communities near the affected waters.
The Department of Health (DOH) has warned against the health risks of exposure to oil spills, whether through inhalation, direct skin contact, or ingestion:

items: Through inhalation: Nausea, eye irritation, increased blood pressure, irregular heart rhythm, headache, loss of appetite, and difficulty concentrating;
Through skin contact: Skin irritation, blisters, burns, peeling skin, and dermatitis;
Through ingestion: Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, coughing, irritability, and unconsciousness. Large amounts may result in convulsions, coma, or death.

blocks.text: As safety precaution, the Health Department advised posting warning signs around affected areas and water bodies, exercising extra caution with drinking water, and keeping children away from the site, as their tendency to put their hands in their mouths puts them at higher risk of accidental ingestion.
The DOH advised individuals exposed to oil to immediately remove and decontaminate contaminated clothing and thoroughly wash affected skin with mild soap and water.
Meanwhile, the DOH urged anyone experiencing symptoms after exposure to an oil spill to seek immediate medical attention at the nearest healthcare facility. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: LTFRB extends regularization application period for 'tempo' TNVS by 30 days
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has extended the application deadline for the regularization of ride-hailing service providers operating under temporary or “tempo”…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 12:03am

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has extended the application deadline for the regularization of ride-hailing service providers operating under temporary or “tempo” status by another 30 days.
The LTFRB previously set a 30-working-day window for online applications, which began on October 8.

Acting upon the directive of Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon, the agency said the extension aims to ensure no one is left behind in the public transportation sector, particularly among Transport Network Vehicle Services (TNVS) operators.

“Our regularization move is aimed at helping thousands of TNVS drivers whose only fault was that they relied in good faith on their onboarding and assumed substantial financial commitments in the process,” LTFRB acting chairman Greg Pua Jr. said.

“Tempo” is known in the transport community, especially in TNVS, as a practice of the Transport Network Companies (TNCs) of onboarding TNVS units on their digital platforms without the units having obtained the requisite authority from the LTFRB.

The agency explained that operating under tempo status violates LTFRB rules and regulations, as it allows TNVS units to offer transport services to the commuting public despite lacking valid authorization.
Based on the latest agency data, the LTFRB has received 13,216 applications, of which 5,091 have already been granted provisional authority.
Pua said the agency is fast-tracking the processing of all applications. He urged applicants to upload all necessary documents to avoid processing delays.

“We ask our partners in the TNVS community who are applying for the regularization to follow the process of the application. The requirements are intended to prevent application cancellations due to some challenges that include questions on vehicle ownership,” Pua said.

Applications for regularization can be submitted through the LTFRB's online platform. Applicants having difficulty complying are advised to reach out to the agency to seek assistance.—Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany: Small plane crashes onto A2 highway, killing 2
articles.summary: Two people have died after a small plane crashed onto Germany's A2 highway near Magdeburg. The crash closed the Hannover-bound lanes on a major east-west route, with no road vehicles reported to be…

image.caption: A small plane crashed into a highway west of Berlin on Friday afternoonImage: Thomas Schulz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt said two people were killed on Friday when a small plane crashed onto the A2 highway northeast of Magdeburg, police said.
The crash closed all Hannover-bound lanes on one of Germany's main east-west routes. Police in Magdeburg said initial findings indicated that no road vehicles were involved.
What do we know about the plane crash?
The aircraft came down at around 2:48 p.m. local time (1348 GMT/UTC) between the town of Burg and the Krahenberge highway rest area.
It caught fire, and emergency crews recovered both occupants dead. The cause of the crash was not immediately known.
Photographs showed firefighters extinguishing the remains of a red-and-white aircraft. Its tail lay on the roadway, with burned wreckage on an embankment.
How was traffic affected?
Police and emergency crews remained at the scene. It was unclear how long the closure would last.
The A2 connects the greater Berlin area with Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia, and is a major route for traffic crossing Germany.

articles.title: Gibo: Filipinos will know those defending China’s false narratives
articles.summary: Those defending China and advancing Beijing’s false narratives for the sake of convenience will be made known to the Filipino people, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am
Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Those defending China and advancing Beijing’s false narratives for the sake of convenience will be made known to the Filipino people, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said yesterday.
Teodoro said there’s no stopping the public from learning the truth.

“The truth will prevail and (some people’s) credibility will suffer,” he said over True FM, adding China’s good faith and sincerity are put to test by Filipino public opinion due to a transparency initiative.
China defenders, he said, should choose to side with the truth and uphold the arbitral award.
He said it all boils down to the nine-dash line which the Arbitral Award rendered void and with no legal effect.

“If you’re advancing a false narrative for the sake of convenience, the people will know and there will be an accounting someday… I mean, this is a free world. It is an open society so the truth will prevail,” he added.
He labeled as falsehood the statements of the Chinese embassy in Manila and its social media posts.
“That’s unprecedented. We actually are responsible in our messaging. They’re the ones who’ve lowered their level and that is worrisome,” he said.
In managing the situation, the secretary emphasized there is no substitute for the truth. “Let’s stick to the truth, the facts on the ground,” he said.
Teodoro said the Philippines has always been careful in managing differences with China, and expects the same kind of responsibility from Beijing.
He slammed Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s statement that the bilateral relationship was facing “malicious interference” by certain Filipino politicians, describing it as “a threat of censorship.”
New arbitration vs China

Political coalition 1Sambayan is urging the Philippine government to pursue a new round of arbitration against China under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to resolve disputes in the West Philippine Sea.

Citing the 2016 arbitral ruling that favored the Philippines and undid China’s nine-dash line, 1Sambayan said the Philippines can file a case to defend the extended continental shelf west of Palawan, Bajo de Masinloc and Ayungin Shoal.

“What this country should seek from the present contest is not a quieter week at sea but a definitive resolution grounded in law – and such a resolution can come from an UNCLOS arbitral tribunal,” the coalition said on Wednesday.

The convention, 1Sambayan said, would better determine the overlapping claims of China, the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia in the extended continental shelf in Palawan, rather than any state that has placed the most hulls in the area.
The coalition also demanded that China be held accountable for the damages suffered by Filipino fisherfolk as a result of its efforts to drive them away from their traditional fishing grounds.
It also offered a different legal approach in addressing the continuing standoff at Ayungin Shoal through the installation of a Coast Guard sub-station to enhance maritime law enforcement.
The coalition underscored that arbitration is among the peaceful means every UN member-state can apply to settle disputes.
“This is not an alternative to standing our ground. It is how a country of our size stands it,” said 1Sambayan. “The law is how we keep it.” — Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: Ex-BARMM lawmaker no-show at PDEA probe
articles.summary: Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang dodged a summons for him to appear on Thursday before the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA), which sought to question him over…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am
Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang

MANILA, Philippines — Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang dodged a summons for him to appear on Thursday before the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA), which sought to question him over a suspected half-ton shipment of shabu from Laos worth about P1.5 billion.
Rimbang was identified by the PDEA and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) as an alleged mastermind and financier of the shipment intercepted by authorities in Laos on Oct. 1.

PDEA spokesman Joseph Frederick Calulut said the agency was investigating the shipment’s links to an international drug syndicate believed to be involved in manufacturing and distributing illegal drugs across the Asia-Pacific region.

“We are still looking at this international drug syndicate. This is a large syndicate operating in the Asia-Pacific region, meaning the Philippines is not its only destination,” Calulut told “Frontline sa Umaga” on TV5 yesterday.
Rimbang had earlier denied the allegations in a video posted on Facebook, claiming they were politically motivated because of his ties to the Duterte family.
In a letter dated Oct. 26, he challenged DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla to release evidence supporting the accusations against him.
Other persons of interest summoned by the PDEA include the shipment’s consignee, identified as Abdulkarim Macalatas, and several unnamed individuals.
Calulut said authorities received an intelligence report from a foreign counterpart in September about renewed cross-border drug smuggling.
The information was relayed to the Bureau of Customs (BOC), which later detected suspected illegal substances in the shipment through X-ray screening and narcotics detection dogs.
He said investigators had identified the names listed as recipients but were still determining the identities of the actual consignees, as such shipments commonly use fictitious names.

The shipment was initially supposed to be claimed by its consignee so authorities could arrest the recipient. However, it was declared abandoned after it remained unclaimed within the period set by the BOC, prompting authorities to conduct a physical inspection.
Calulut said investigators had yet to establish whether the drugs seized in Laos and the shipment intercepted in the Philippines came from the same laboratory, although both originated from Laos.

articles.title: Nurse shortage could reach 250,000 by 2030 – CHED
articles.summary: The shortage of nurses could reach 250,000 by 2030 if current figures of 127,000 to 190,000 nurse deficit in 2025 continue, Commission on Higher Education (CHED) Chairperson Shirley Agrupis said…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am

Third year nursing students of University of Perpetual Help System receive their caps and pins during the university's 43rd thanksgiving and commitment rites at Ernesto Crisostomo Palanca Hall in Las Piñas City on June 21, 2023.
STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — The shortage of nurses could reach 250,000 by 2030 if current figures of 127,000 to 190,000 nurse deficit in 2025 continue, Commission on Higher Education (CHED) Chairperson Shirley Agrupis said yesterday.

In her speech during the ceremonial turnover of the Philippine Nursing Education Roadmap 2020 in Ortigas, Agrupis said that while the Philippines has long been recognized for producing skilled and competent nurses who serve both in the country and abroad, there continues to be a significant lack in the national health care system.

“Estimates cited in the Roadmap place the shortage at 127,000 to 190,000 nurses as of 2025, potentially reaching 250,000 by 2030 if current trends continue. This makes the work of strengthening nursing education even more important,” Agrupis said.
An estimated 200,000 Filipinos live and work in the United Kingdom, including more than 35,000 Filipino nurses serving in its National Health Service.

“We want to continue preparing our nurses for international opportunities through quality education and professional development, while also strengthening our own health care workforce. These priorities must go together,” Agrupis added.
She said the Philippine Nursing Education Roadmap provides the government with a framework.

“The findings point to important areas for improvement: curriculum relevance and clinical preparedness, faculty development, student welfare, institutional resources, research capacity and alignment with workforce requirements,” Agrupis said.
She added that the country currently has 434 higher education institutions offering BS Nursing programs nationwide.
“We must continue addressing differences in resources and capacity to ensure that students across regions receive quality nursing education and adequate clinical preparation,” she said.

Meanwhile, nearly 200 Filipino nurses and careworker candidates are undergoing Japanese language training ahead of their deployment to hospitals and caregiving facilities in Japan under its bilateral labor agreement with the Philippines.
The 198 candidates are the 19th batch under the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement and their preparatory training formally opened on Nov. 4.
One hundred twenty-one will attend online language classes, while the remaining 77 will receive face-to-face instruction. The six-month program covers Japanese language, culture and social etiquette.

The candidates will undergo another six months of Japanese language training upon arrival in Japan before beginning their assignments. The training programs are provided free of charge under the government-to-government deployment arrangement.
The candidates will take Japan’s national examination for nurses or certified careworkers while gaining professional experience at Japanese health care facilities. — Christine Boton

articles.title: VP’s SALN, AMLC records formally admitted into evidence
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has formally admitted into evidence the statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) and Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte conducts a press conference in Mandaluyong on February 18, 2026.
STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court has formally admitted into evidence the statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) and Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records of Vice President Sara Duterte, while denying the prosecution’s plea to include Commission on Audit (COA) reports regarding her controversial confidential funds.

In a 21-page order issued Thursday, presiding officer Francis Escudero resolved the prosecution’s formal offer of documentary evidence on Article II (unexplained wealth), defining the exact legal parameters of the trial.

To evaluate the Vice President’s wealth, the court admitted volumes of financial, corporate, tax and property documents dating from 2007 to 2021, overruling the defense’s continuing objection against the use of records that pre-date Duterte’s vice presidency.
However, the tribunal imposed a strict limitation on how these older documents can be used by the senator-judges.
“Records predating June 30, 2022 cannot be used to charge or prove additional, independent offenses committed before the Respondent’s current term as Vice President,” Escudero ruled.

Instead, the tribunal explained that these records are admitted “SOLELY to establish a factual baseline against which the Respondent’s assets, liabilities, net worth, financial resources, transactions and business interests during 2022 to 2025 may be evaluated under Article II.”

On the other hand, it completely excluded all exhibits intended to show that the COA flagged and disallowed disbursements of confidential funds in the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education in 2022 and 2023.

The court also admitted AMLC intelligence reports, covered transaction reports and suspicious transaction reports involving the Vice President, her husband Manases Carpio and their associated businesses. — Bella Cariaso, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Socmed affecting public perception of VP impeachment
articles.summary: Public opinion of the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is largely affected by information being shared on social media, a political scientist said.

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am

Political analyst Cleve Arguelles points to a shift in public opinion on Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, citing Momentum Research’s October survey, which found that 39 percent of Filipinos favor her conviction, while 34 percent support her acquittal.
MANILA, Philippines — Public opinion of the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is largely affected by information being shared on social media, a political scientist said.

In an interview with The STAR’s “Truth on the Line,” political scientist Cleve Arguelles, founder of public opinion research firm Momentum Research, described the ongoing proceedings as the country’s “first social media impeachment trial.”

“Most Filipinos would say that they watch it through clips online, spliced videos. Meaning, our people are seeing the senator-judges using the lens of partisan edits and biased spliced videos. That affects the public opinion as well,” he noted.

Arguelles said less than a majority of Filipinos closely follow Duterte’s impeachment trial, which could mean that the public may be making judgments without being fully informed of the progress of the trial.
“The distractions, the big voices online, that affect their opinion of the trial,” he pointed out.
The latest Momentum survey conducted from Oct. 16 to 19 found that almost four in 10 respondents support Duterte’s conviction.
Asked whether the impeachment court should acquit or convict Duterte on the charge of unexplained wealth, 38.8 percent said the senator-judges must vote to convict.
Some 33.8 percent were in favor of acquittal, while 22.6 percent said they do not know. The remaining 4.7 percent declined to respond.

articles.title: Make Christmas goods affordable, President Marcos tells execs
articles.summary: President Marcos has ordered government officials to make basic commodities affordable this Christmas season, while urging public institutions to keep holiday parties simple as the country prepares…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has ordered government officials to make basic commodities affordable this Christmas season, while urging public institutions to keep holiday parties simple as the country prepares for the effects of a super El Niño.
Marcos gave the directive as he administered the oath of office to 10 ad interim Cabinet officials and agency heads during a ceremony at Malacañang yesterday.

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, who was among those who took their oath, said the administration is focused on helping Filipino families celebrate Christmas with less worry over rising prices and the cost of daily necessities.

“Hopefully, food prices will continue to drop and, most importantly, Noche Buena will be affordable for everyone. That is the President’s primary instruction,” Recto told reporters in a chance interview at the Palace.

Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon and Public Works Secretary Giovanni Lopez, who also took their oath before Marcos, vowed to strengthen coordination to ease traffic congestion and improve public transportation, particularly during the holiday rush.
Dizon said Marcos wants commuters to spend less time on the road and save on transportation costs, especially during the busy Christmas season.

To accommodate the expected surge in passengers, Dizon revealed that the Department of Transportation plans to deploy additional buses, trains and other public transport services to provide commuters with more convenient and accessible travel options.
Palace press officer Claire Castro, meanwhile, urged government agencies to keep their Christmas parties simple as part of the government’s austerity measures.

“The austerity measures remain in effect to this day. While we are not issuing an order regarding Christmas parties, we would like to remind everyone to keep them simple, as there are still many other pressing issues that we need to address,” she said.

articles.title: Prosecution seeks protection for 55 witnesses in Duterte trial
articles.summary: The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has formally requested judges to provide protective measures to 55 witnesses involved in the crimes against humanity case against former…

blocks.text: November 7, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has formally requested judges to provide protective measures to 55 witnesses involved in the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

In a 12-page request originally filed on Oct. 30 and released on Friday, ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said there is an “objectively justifiable risk” that applies to several witnesses and others involved in the case.

“In-court protective measures and special measures are required in order to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses that will testify before the Chamber,” read the request.

“Mr. Duterte will not be unfairly prejudiced by the measures requested. The measures sought are proportionate and constitute the least restrictive means necessary to fairly balance Mr. Duterte’s right to a fair and public trial against the Court’s competing obligation to protect the interests of victims and witnesses who appear before it,” it added.

The witnesses were divided into six categories: insider witnesses residing in the Philippines, crime-based witnesses residing in the Philippines, witnesses in the Philippines, witnesses residing abroad, witnesses admitted in the ICC protection program and prosecution staff members.

The prosecution requested three types of in-court protective and special measures for the trial witnesses. These include measures intended to protect a witness’ identity from the public, closed or private session intended to protect particular portions of a witness’ testimony from public disclosure and measures intended to support a witness psychologically during testimony.
Based on the request, the prosecution wanted the protective measures to be in the form of pseudonyms, face and voice distortion and permitted private session.

It said that stringent in-court protective measures for the witnesses “will ensure that they can give evidence freely without fear for their personal safety and without compromising their security or the security of their family members.”
Two witnesses to be presented by the prosecution are its staff members. Details of the nature of their testimony have yet to be released.

For its part, the Philippine National Police is prepared to provide security to witnesses in the crimes against humanity cases against former president Duterte before the ICC, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said yesterday.
Nartatez said the police have yet to receive any communication from the ICC regarding the protection of the witnesses.
“I do not know who these witnesses are. We have also not received any letter from the ICC,” Nartatez said at Camp Crame.

Meanwhile, National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag said they are hopeful they can arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa anytime soon, with its search unit continuing efforts to locate the senator, who has been in hiding since May.
Matibag said operatives were pursuing leads and verifying information on his whereabouts, but declined to disclose more details .

articles.title: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
articles.summary: The Trump administration had hoped the construction of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.

blocks.text: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch
ByNardine Saad and Isabella JewellReporting fromMemorial Circle
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.
The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."
"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.
Image source, Reuters
An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery

A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.
It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".
The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.
The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.

Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".

items: How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image

blocks.text: He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the arch

blocks.text: Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the arch
Opponents have strongly disagreed.
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."

Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.

blocks.caption: Satellite image with 3D buildings visible showing a model of the proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington DC, positioned south of the Potomac River at the end of Arlington Memorial Bridge. The Lincoln Memorial, on the other side of the bridge, the Washington Monument, further to the east, and the Wh…

blocks.text: Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.

Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.

It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.title: Fact check: Three viral Iran war posts debunked
articles.summary: In the wake of the new US attack on Iran, social media is awash with dramatic images and claims about the fighting. DW Fact Check found AI-generated and recycled videos, as well as misleading posts…

image.caption: Disinformation narratives are often triggered by real news events, such as the latest Iran war escalationImage: U.S. Central Command/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The reason we lost is the war," US Vice President JD Vance said, shortly after Republicans suffered major losses during the US midterm elections in both the House and Senate. He was referring to the US-Israel war against Iran.
Hours before the US midterms, the US reportedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island, despite Trump previously saying that there would be no new strikes before the elections.
Among fears of a renewed regional escalation, social media has been flooded with dramatic images and purported battlefield updates. Not all of them are genuine.
DW Fact check takes a closer look at three viral claims.
No Iranian missile drone attack on US aircraft carrier

Claim: In this post on X, a user claims that Iran launched a massive missile and drone attack on a US aircraft carrier, resulting in fatalities. It is accompanied by a video showing an explosion and its aftermath on what appears to be an aircraft carrier. The post has garnered over 643.000 views.

blocks.caption: Hectic camera movements can conceal glitches in AI-generated materialImage: X

blocks.text: Verdict: Fake
The 15-second video is an AI-generated fake.

Although there have been reports of Iranian forces attempting to shoot down a US aircraft, there have been no credible reports of a successful attack on a US aircraft carrier which resulted in fatalities.
The AI video also predates the latest US strikes — it has circulated at least since May this year. At that time, it was shared alongside a different claim unrelated to the current situation.

Frame-by-frame analysis reveals several inconsistencies. At approximately three seconds in, the feet of a running person visually glitch. The sea in the background appears uniform and almost video game-like. At five seconds, several people appear to pass through one another, and their limbs also glitch.

The voices in the audio sound synthetic and appear closely synchronized with the visuals. Both AI Detection tools by Meta AI and Google Gemini identified strong indicators that the video was AI-generated. It is important to note, however, that such tools provide an assessment of likelihood, rather than definitive proof that something was created using AI.
The video is considerably shaky and short, two characteristics that warrant closer scrutiny of possible AI use.
The visual nature of supposedly chaotically filmed videos can cover up glitches that still happen frequently in AI-generated content.
Fact check: How AI videos hijack your emotions in 8 seconds
A burning building in South Korea, not US bases in the Gulf

Claim: This user on X shares a video with the claim that "Iran attacks the US bases in the Gulf." A burning building is visible with large dark plumes of smoke rising from it. It has been viewed over 55.000 times.

blocks.caption: Striking images are frequently recycled to illustrate unrelated eventsImage: X

blocks.text: Verdict: Misleading
A reverse image search shows that the images are recycled and show a fire in South Korea in 2025.

News reports indicated that a fire broke out at a Fashion Logistics Center in Cheonan. The same building is visible in the street-level view of South Korea’s Naver Maps street imagery, and its location matches the red building in a mountainous area which is shown on Google Maps satellite imagery.
Visual cues that match include the building itself, the white lettering "E-Land fashion" on the right side and the mountains in the background.

The reverse image search also reveals that the video has repeatedly circulated. It made rounds in July this year attached to Iran war posts in Tamil and English with one post on X reaching 1.4 million views. Other posts linked it to the war in Yemenand other conflicts, unrelated to the fire in South Korea.
Content farm's posts reach millions
Claim: "Iran has launched a major hypersonic missile attack targeting multiple Israeli military bases," an X account writes. By the time of writing, the post had 2.5 million views.

blocks.caption: Content farms are designed to produce large amounts of cheap, attention-grabbing contentImage: X

blocks.text: Iran claims to have hypersonic missiles and has previously claimed to have fired Fattah-1 missiles at Israel, most recently in June 2025. There are no credible reports about Iranian hypersonic missile attacks during the latest escalation.

The account that has published the claim has over 100.000 followers and posts with high frequency, often over ten times a day. Most of the posts reach hundred thousands of views, often using urgent "Breaking" headlines and repeating similar posts. In one post for example, it claims "the war has officially started" reaching more than 30 million views. These are all hallmarks of a so-called "content farm."

In a comment to DW, analyst Charlene Lin from the internet watchdog NewsGuard writes that this account is a South-Asia based content farm. The account has already been flagged in relation to other disinformation narratives.
Lin writes that such South Asia-based content farms "seem to spread false claims about geopolitics by typically posing as pro-China/Russia/Iran users."
She adds that the account amplifies false claims alongside other accounts that appear to be part of the same network, typically within a short period of time.

Victoire Rio, an expert on social-media monetization and information integrity, wrote to DW that "it's pretty common to see financially-motivated actors from South and Southeast Asia leverage prominent news issues to generate a financial profit off the engagement on platforms like X."

articles.title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
articles.summary: No link has been established between the threats against the airlines and those against the media outlets.

blocks.text: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.

Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".

In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.

The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years over 191 murders
articles.summary:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over the deaths of 190 children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

blocks.caption: Kenyan homicide detectives and forensic experts examine exhumed bodies in Shakahola forest. Photograph: EPA

blocks.text: In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting
